subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DEATH OF SIX OFFICERS WHILE PRISONERS OF WAR IN GERMANY

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs): On behalf of the Secretary of State for External Affairs I wish to take this opportunity to inform the house with deep regret of a shocking incident involving the death of six officers of the Royal Canadian Air Force who were prisoners of war in Germany, at a camp near Dresden, Stalag Luft III. The following statement was made

War Policy
in the British House of Commons this morning by the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, Mr. Eden.
I deeply regret to have to tell the house that his majesty's government have received information from the protecting power that forty-seven air force offices of the Royal Air Force and of the Royal Canadian, Australian, New ' Zealand and South African air forces have been shot by the Germans after a mass escape from Stalag Luft III.
According to the information given to a representative of the protecting power by the German authorities, in the course of a routine visit to this camp on the 17th April, seventy-six officers had escaped from Stalag Luft III on the 22nd March.
Of these seventy-six officers fifteen had been recaptured, fourteen were still at large and forty-seven had been shot, some whilst resisting arrest and some in the course of a new attempt to escape after capture.
His majesty's government are profoundly shocked at this news and have urgently requested the protecting power to demand from the German government a full and immediate report of the circumstances in which these men met their death and an explanation of its failure to report the facts at once to the protecting power.
The names of the officers shot were furnished to the representative of the protecting power on the occasion of his visit and the next of kin have been informed.
The house will wish me to express its deep sympathy with the relatives of these most gallant men.
That is the end of Mr. Eden's statement. There are some points I wish to add. First, the next of kin of the members of the Royal Canadian Air Force who thus met their deaths have been informed, and their names have been given to the press. Second, as soon as word was received in Ottawa the Canadian government joined in the urgent request to the protecting power mentioned in Mr. Eden's statement, that a full and immediate report of the circumstances be demanded from the German government, and an explantion of the failure to report the facts at once to the protecting power. Third, I am sure I shall be expressing the feeling of the Canadian government and of this house when I say that we too are profoundly shocked at this news and that we wish to extend our deep sympathy and regret to the relatives of the brave Canadians who lost their lives in these distressing circumstances.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF DEATH OF SIX OFFICERS WHILE PRISONERS OF WAR IN GERMANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join with the minister in the words of sympathy he has uttered for the next of kin who have been aggrieved as he has announced to-day. It just shows the type of people we are fighting in this war. And more than that, may I say it shows, too, in bold contrast, the difference
between the way the Germans have treated those prisoners and the way we have treated their prisoners over here.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: MOTION, MR. POULIOT, FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 31
speechtext:
The hon. member gave me a copy of the motion before I came to the house, I have not had sufficient time to look through Hansard to ascertain what may have happened in connection with this subject now brought before the house by the hon. member's motion. However, standing order 31 provides in subsection 6(c) that-
The motion must not revive discussion on a matter which has been discussed in the same session.
I rely upon my memory as to what happened in that connection, and I have recollection of many occasions upon which this matter, now placed before the house by the hon, member, has been discussed by the house.
Subsection 6(d), as found at page 64 of Beauchesne's Third Edition, states:
The motion must not anticipate a matter which has been previously appointed for consideration by the house, or with reference to which a notice of motion has been previously given and not withdrawn.
In the proceedings before the house there is on the order paper an order which has been the subject of discussion since March, namely, a resolution to introduce a measure to provide sums of money for the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada. The subject now before us might well be discussed under that measure. My recollection is that it has been discussed in the house; but whether it has or has not, the fact remains that there is a resolution before the house which at a later stage will be transformed into a bill. The subject matter of the motion now made by the hon. member could well be discussed either on second reading of the bill which would follow that resolution, or in committee of the whole.
But my thought is that I should try to bring to the consciousness of the house the fact that a motion such as this does not seem to me to be covered at all by standing order 31.
I would point out that that standing order provides for the discussion of a matter of "urgent public importance". This is what we find in paragraph ISO as it appears at page 78 of Beauchesne's Third Edition, respecting the practice in the British House of Commons:
Standing order 10 of the United Kingdom House in force since 1882, also provides that a member may propose the adjournment of the house "for the purpose of discussing a matter of urgent public importance." On the 13th of April, 1894, a member asked leave to make that motion to discuss "the neglect of the government
LMr. Pouliot.l
to take measures for the relief of agricultural depression during the present session." As forty members rose in support of the motion, debate was alloAved, but on its conclusion, the Speaker said: "I do not think that, under the Standing Order of 1882. a motion on a subject of this kind, having such a very wide scope, was ever Contemplated. What I think was contemplated, was an occurrence of some sudden emergency, either in home or in foreign affairs. But I do not think it was contemplated-if the-bouse will -allow me to state my views-that a question of very wide scope, which would demand legislation to deal with it in any effective manner, should be the subject of discussion on a motion for the adjournment of the house, because, if that was so, we might have repeated motions made by the opposition of the day, not so much in the direction of censoring the government for action -which had -been taken or not -taken, for bringing to notice some grievance demanding instant remedy, as in the direction of wishing to introduce legislation on some particular subject. That is not the purpose of the Standing Order of 1882, and would, I think, cut at tile root of the order."
In my view the purpose of our standing order 31 is not that contained in the proposals offered in the hon. member's motion. For that reason I rule it is not of sufficient public importance to justify the adjournment of the house.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Munitions and' Supply. Has the minister received a letter dated May 16 from the -united steel workers of America at Oshawa, Ontario, asking -that he rec-onsider his proposed transfer of the shell case contract from the Pedlar plant -at Oshawa to a Montreal firm? If so, will -the minister tell the house what decision, if any, he has made? In the event the minister proceeds with his transfer proposals, will he tell -the house why? Will the minister also tell the house what precautions he is taking to safeguard -the interests of -the nearly 400 employees who stand to lose their jobs, their seniority, their homes and the advantages which they have gained through specialized training for particular kinds of work?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
speakerposition: Minister of Munitions and Supply
subtopic: PEDLAR PLANT, OSHAWA-MOSQUITO PLANE PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member
was good enough to give me notice of his question. The situation at the Pedlar plant at Oshawa is that the plant is one of three holding contracts for the manufacture of 40-millimetre cartridge cases. A reduction in the demand for that type of cartridge case has

Selective Service
occurred, and the ordinary practice is to curtail production at the point of the greatest labour shortage, which, happens to be Oshawa.
There is a tremendous demand in that city for man-power for the Mosquito programme, which is the highest priority programme we have on hand at the moment. The Oshawa plant is not being closed, but its work is being curtailed. The men who will not be required are being transferred to the Mosquito programme in the same city. Sufficient work is left in the Pedlar plant to take care of all those workmen who do not come up to the high physical standards required in the Mosquito programme. The result is that no labour will be displaced, as far as residence is concerned, and no hardship will be suffered.
The men who will be transferred will be the more recent employees of the Pedlar plant and they will receive work at somewhat higher wages than those obtaining in the Pedlar plant. I think this answers the question. There is no transfer of any contract from Oshawa to Montreal. The interests of the employees are being completely safeguarded.

speakerposition: topic

speechtext:
The house resumed from Thursday, May 18, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to His Majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war-Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.
PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH Pensions branch-
Treatment and pension examinations-members and ex-members of the armed forces (present war), $9,000,000.

Mr. Chairman, questions affecting the Department of Pensions and National Health are the most important we have to consider at the present time outside of winning the war. Our men and women who are over there doing the fighting must be taken care of after they come back, and I feel that this house and Canadians as a whole will be neglecting their duty if adequate provision is not made for them.
A number of vitally important questions have been discussed in this debate, and it is not my intention to go into them in detail to-day because I think the minister realizes how important they are. I shall take just a few moments to add1 my words in support of those that were spoken yesterday on behalf of the members of our armed forces.
One of the points I wish to emphasize has to do with preenlistment conditions. We find that a number of men who are discharged from the services are not fairly dealt with because of their categorization upon discharge.

When a man goes into the army and undergoes all the examinations he has to have before he can get very far in the service, and then is discharged and put in a lower category, the government of this country should be responsible for taking care of him.
Another question that was brought up yesterday and is deserving of consideration is the setting up of health centres for restoring to health the men when returning from overseas. It has been pointed out that in eastern, central and western Canada we have those health centres. I want to say a few words here for the prairie provinces. I think most of the members realize that we have an invigorating climate in the prairie provinces that does wonders for the health of those who have been accustomed to living there, and I would urge upon the minister that he see to it that a health centre is established in at least one of the three prairie provinces.
The removal of the insurance principle from the Pension Act in 1940 is doing a grave injustice. I would strongly urge that that principle be reinstated, and, further, that it be made retroactive to the time it was taken ou* of the act-because, as was pointed out yesterday and has been repeatedly pointed out on different occasions, grave injustices have been done bo ' the men, their wives and families, because of the removal of this protection. The only reason I can see for ever taking that clause out of the act was to save money to the treasury. It has been demonstrated that we have plenty of money with which to recruit these men, to train and equip them, to feed and transport them to and from the war area, and I cannot see any valid reason why adequate pensions should not be provided for them when they return. On more than one occasion since the war broke out the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance have expropriated, if I may use that word, one of the slogans of the social crediters and told us that what is physically possible must be made financially possible. I contend that Canada can provide adequate pensions for her returned men, and if it is physically possible to do that, it is financially possible. There is another slogan: Give us the tools and we will finish the job. I think we have all the tools and all the requirements necessary to provide the things that are needed for our returned men. Let us see that the job is finished in proper fashion.

Mr. Chairman, the
estimates before us are of the utmost importance to the men and women in our armed forces, and through them to all of us in Canada. We have legislation that is broad

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
in its scope and splendid in its application, although there are criticisms made in which I join; nevertheless the legislation stands as very broad in its scope. But no legislation alone, no matter how good, can give to our veterans that respected place in the life of our country which we feel is their due and which we so earnestly desire that they should have. To attain that place there are two things that are beyond the reach of legislation. There must be, first, an understanding appreciation from us who remain at home, especially from those in the veteran's own family circle. That is where women have a job which no one else can do, and which no legislation can achieve.
Secondly, much depends upon the veteran's own adaptability in taking advantage of the opportunities offered to him in fitting himself again into the life of the community and of the nation. Neither of these conditions is easy to fulfil.
The soldiers, many of them, left as boys. They come back as men. Without war, their outlook would have changed during these years from adolencence to manhood. With war, they have still more far-reaching problems of readjustment, both mental and emotional. Let us never forget when dealing with individual cases that these men are fundamentally sound in their approach to life, but may need time in which to regain their civilian equilibrium. The girls they left behind them are women now and are taking a very real part in Canada's war effort, some in uniform, many in industry or on the farm, and some just continuing that tremendously important work of looking after the homes and the children. They, too, have a different outlook. It seems to me that we need all the patience we have and all the tolerance and understanding possible in making adjustments in our homes and on a national scale. I repeat that the men and women are fundamentally sound. The more quickly the returned men come back into the stream of ordinary everyday activities, of their own volition-and individually that may take a little time-the more quickly will the invisible scars of battle be healed. We honour them, men and women, and they know that we honour them. We, who are the thousands of individual citizens, must do our part to give every opportunity for readjustment. Now that, Mr. Chairman, is beyond legislation. But there is much that is within the scope of legislation. That is why I find the broad lines for reestablishment so satisfactory. Oh, I know that there are places where changes are needed. Members from all sides of the house have given advice along these lines and
the minister knows how untiringly I have taken up individual cases as well as policies with him and the members of his department. These matters are under review. Some have already been corrected, and consideration will be given to others.
But the training facilities, educational and vocational, are the best forms of reestablishment that can be given. Here is provision for the student, the artisan, the skilled worker, the labourer, the farmer, to master the tools of his trade. He will be put in a good position to carry on through the coming years and to catch up, as much as possible, with developments. I shall not take time to review all the opportunities offered. There seems to be something for almost every case.
I am particularly gratified that we have extended the principle of allowances paid for wives and children into the post-war period. Regular service dependents' living allowances are made during the training period, whether educational or vocational training is taken, and allowances are paid during the time that returns are awaited. This is of tremendous significance. It fits the income more directly to the need. It breaks down some of the resistance or disinclination to going back to school. That will not be easy, you know. It recognizes the contribution made by women and children to the war effort and to the life of the nation. That same right to allowances applies if a veteran needs hospitalization for war wounds in later years. The policy is of great importance in our progress towards raising the standard of living.
Right now may I pay tribute to the women who have taken on unusual responsibilities outside of their homes and whose work was praised by the Minister of Labour last week; also to the home makers whose work has remained much the same in raising their families and in making life happy for their men folk. Sir William Beveridge has said this:
In any measure of social policy in which regard is had to facts, the great majority of married women must be regarded as occupied on work which is vital though unpaid, without which their husbands could not do their paid work, and without w'hich the nation could not continue.
Homemakers take part just as much as office and professional workers in the life of the community. Their horizon is not limited. They are interested in public affairs. The walls of a house do not confine the mind. We claim the right to be full partners in a free country. What affects the men affects in almost equal measure the women.
The lines of Canadian policy were laid down early in the war, were altered and

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
improved upon, and will be still further improved upon as the weeks go by. It is interesting to note that the United States congress is now debating some of the plans which were settled policy with us some time ago. For instance, I have here a cutting from a Philadelphia paper which contains this paragraph, under dateline Washington, May 7, 1944:
Topping the house programme ds the "G.I. Bill of Rights", passed by the senate before the Easter recess and rewritten by the house veterans committee. Debate starting Thursday is expected to centre on proposals for unemployment compensation and educational benefits for discharged men and women.
These are things we already have, in Canada.
The senate voted for 52 weeks of unemployment pay at rates varying with family status from $15 to $25; the house committee cut this to 20 weeks and set a flat compensation of $20. The committee also rewrote the education provision _ and in doing so drew the fire of educational leaders who assailed the action as a menace to educational freedom.
Thus they are taking up a line which already is our settled policy. The lines of our policy are the lines recommended at the International Labour Organization conference in Philadelphia, which I had the privilege of attending this month. This twenty-sixth session of the I.L.O. will go down in history as one of the most important discussions ever to be undertaken, by delegations from forty-one countries, representing government, employers' and workers' groups. In the historic city of Philadelphia, where the Bill of Rights was written for the American nation and where the first United States Congress held its meetings from 1780 to 1790, was written a new Philadelphia bill of rights for international justice and prosperity.
One of the ten committees there dealt with reestablishment of veterans. I am glad to say that the Canadian delegation was in agreement with almost every part of that policy. It was stated very much on the lines of our own established policy. It asked for training. It emphasized that the best reestablishment policy is the one which puts the returned man in a position to hold his own in civilian life, with training and retraining, and pay and allowances to provide for that period.
As you know, there were three groups of delegates from each country participating- government, employers and workers. Each expressed the greatest determination and anxiety to see fair play for the returned men. Sometimes they differed as to the means to be used, but the objective was the same. I wish you might have heard Mr. Tomlinson,

head of the government delegation from the United Kingdom and joint parliamentary secretary of the British ministry of labour and national service, tell what is being done there for amputation cases, for example. He said that no man need fear that he would not be given all the care humanly possible and the appliances to fit him for work again. He himself had seen men who had lost both hands and both legs, taking their part in rehabilitation exercises. I wish our minister would take the time to tell us what Canada is doing along that line. When it was suggested that a clause be deleted from the recommendations which asked that a quota of amputation cases be included in factory payrolls, it was an employer who spoke for his group and asked that the clause be left there. He said employers were anxious to give all cooperation to reestablish those disabled, that the best ones would anyway, and that by such a provision the careless employers would realize their obligation.
We are glad that at Edmonton the military hospital facilities have been extended. We are also pleased that government house may be taken over as a convalescent home. I hope the minister will tell us something more of the progress which has been made there and as to what is contemplated in the near future.
We have heard many criticisms of the policy that Canada is following, and we do want some alterations. When I was home at Easter I met with ex-servicemen, and we discussed complaints. There were many. I am taking them up with the department. They told me also that they had written to express their opinion to Mr. Woods. I have here a copy of a letter which was sent to Mr. Woods, and as that letter is in direct opposition to some of the things I have heard I would like to read it to you:
616 McLeod Building, Edmonton, Alberta,
Walter S. Woods, Esq., Associate Deputy Minister, Department of Pensions and National Health,
Ottawa, Canada.
March 31, 1944.
Dear Mr. Woods:
At the weekly meeting of this committee held on the 29th instant Mr. W. R. McLaren, welfare officer here, attended our meeting and gave our committee a most informative and interesting account of the procedure laid down by your department upon general demobilization of the armed forces and particularly regarding casualties; also as to rehabilitation.
At the close of this discussion our committee unanimously Tesolved that this letter should be written to you expressing the appreciation of our committee as to the apparent care and trouble which has.been taken by your department regarding this procedure and also to say

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
that the committee realizes that your department is keeping a very open mind to suggestions regarding discharge and rehabilitation.
With kindest personal regards, I am Yours sincerely,
S. C. S. Kerr,
Chairman,
Edmonton Ex-Service Men's Rehabilitation Committee.
That committee has on it representatives of the Amputations Association, Army and Navy Veterans Association, British Imperial Comrades, Canadian Corps Association, Canadian Legion B.E.S.L. No. 24, Canadian Legion B.E.S.L. No. 27, the Red Chevron club, and also representatives of the central committee of the women's auxiliaries in Edmonton. It is therefore, as you see, a comprehensive body.
Here is another little extract, from the Edmonton Journal, April IS, 1944, which I should read. It deals with an address given in Vermilion and is as follows:
Says Canada's War Pension Plan Best
Vermilion.-War pension system in Canada is regarded by S. C. Heckbert, provincial president of the Canadian Legion, as the "best in the world". He said so at a dinner meeting of the Legion branch here this week in celebration of Vimy, with more than 100 ex-servicemen, their wives, and members of the ladies' auxiliary present.
Recent legislation by the dominion parliament, said Mr. Heckbert, has facilitated rehabilitation of servicemen and had provided in some measure for the education of those who had dropped their own educational plans or civilian work to enlist for the war. He pointed out, however, that citizens in general have direct responsibility in facing post-war problems.
We are faced with a good many problems- new problems, such as were mentioned by the Minister of Justice this afternoon, pressing problems arising out of casualties overseas, the absence of the men overseas, and all these different things. But I was impressed at Philadelphia with how much greater problems the occupied nations face than we do. The depth and magnitude of the problems confronting these people are far beyond ours. They have our difficulties, and many more peculiar to themselves-armed enemy forces in their own country, all these atrocities and other terrible episodes of which we read. In talking, for instance, to one of the members of the delegation from Luxembourg he said, speaking of conditions in his own country, that Luxembourg has been incorporated into the German state, and that their men were being conscripted and sent to fight on the Russian front; that hundreds of their -men had fallen already, fighting side by side with the Germans against the Russians. It seems to me that that is about the bitterest touch of all-to have to fight with vour enemies
against your friends. We do not have to face such problems, thanks to the magnificent stand made in our behalf as well as theirs by our allies, and thanks also to the courage, the endurance and the heroism of our own men. We must see to it that we do all we can in the way of rehabilitation and reestablishment and carry on the policy with vigour and with understanding.

A number of new and valuable suggestions in the interests of the members of our armed forces have been made during the discussion of this item by several members of the committee. I was particularly impressed by the suggestion made by the member for Vancouver South that our Pension Act be amended to include a provision similar to that contained in the British regulations, which provide, first, that it shall be presumed that a man's condition as recorded on his admission to the service was in fact his condition at that time, and second that it shall be presumed that any deterioration in a man's condition after his admission is due to his service.
These presumptions would of course be presumptions of evidence and would be rebuttable; but in my opinion they would make for justice and fair play. It happens too often that a man who is admitted to the armed services and who passes his physical and medical examinations and is qualified as A-l, on applying for pension is informed that he is suffering from a preenlistment disability, or a preenlistment ailment. Such a finding hardly makes sense, and it is a reflection, it seems to me, on the army doctors who made the examinations when he was admitted into the service.
I was interested recently in a case in which a man who had been classified as A-l afterwards contracted a disease and applied for pension. When he went before the board he was informed that his ailment was of preenlistment origin. He went before a second board and that- board said that his ailment was not of preenlistment origin but had developed during his service, though not in the course of his duty. He then went before the appeal court and they granted him a pension. If our act contained a provision similar to the British regulations I do not think that inconsistent findings of this kind would have been made. An amendment such as is proposed would clarify the procedure. It would help the board to carry on its work and make its findings and would assist members of the armed forces, who are obliged to apply for pensions, to obtain those pensions when they

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
are entitled to them. I would urge upon the minister that he accept the suggestion of the member for Vancouver South and recommend that this provision of the British regulations be inserted in our Pension Act.

At the risk of tiring the committee by repeating what has already been said, I wish to refer for a few moments again to Christie street hospital. I do so because that institution is of vital importance to a large number of my constituents, those who returned from the last war and families of those who are serving in this one.
Yesterday a minor attempt was made in the house to determine which of the two older political parties was responsible for Christie street hospital being where and what it is. I submit that it is no longer a question of party responsibility and that nothing can be gained by attempting to assign that responsibility to one party or the other. The fact is that that hospital to-day, notwithstanding all the improvement that has been introduced, notwithstanding the excellent quality of help and the calibre and ability of the medical men who are serving there, remains a disgrace to this government and to every former government that has had any part in maintaining it where it is. The choice of the hospital in the first place and the continuance of it now, as well as the attempt to make it apparently a permanent hospital, does no credit to any government or to any political party. In my opinion it shows a callous disregard of the welfare of the personnel of our armed forces who are unfortunate enough to require hospital treatment.
No amount of money, no amount of improvement, no amount of devotion on the part of the employees, no amount of skill on the part of the doctors, can ever make that hospital a satisfactory one for the returned men so long as it remains where it is to-day. The only way in which it can be made satisfactory, standing where it does, would be by the introduction of an enormous clearance scheme which would move the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway tracks, which would move the steel yard situated right across the road, and which would move the factories situated within a few feet of the hospital.
And still there would not be a park at hand.

Unless homes and other buildings were demolished and parks created there would be no park space for the patients in the hospital. As has already been 6tated, the hospital is situated on a factory

site. As a matter of fact, the old original hospital was I believe a biscuit factory at the time it was taken over. It is situated seventy-five feet from the right of way of a through freight line of the Canadian Pacific. It is situated beside a number of sidings and switches, and it is immediately across the street from steel yards where cranes and donkey engines are operating all day long, and all night long as well, with the aid of searchlights.
The wards are overlooked on two sides by a factory and a warehouse and on a third by this steel yard. The building, originally a factory building, is a fire trap. Any visitor to the hospital can discover that wooden floors were originally laid on the steel beams. As other members have pointed out, there is much in the building that is easily destructible by fire. Because of the noise, the sickest and most helpless patients are usually located on the top storey of the building, and if there were ever a fire in that building considerable difficulty would be experienced in getting many of these helpless patients down from the top floor.
I cannot understand, nor can anyone who has any connection with that hospital understand, why that building was ever retained as a military hospital. I am confident that the public served by it, both military and civilian, would have supported the government wholeheartedly if it had demolished the building and used the funds that have been expended from time to time to extend and improve it to build another hospital in a more suitable place. Of course the minister has given us various explanations from time to time for not having followed that procedure. Once he blamed it on the difficulty of getting building material, a matter which 1m said was not under the control of the Canadian government alone but which concerned the United States government as well. I do not believe anyone in this country will accept that as a reasonable excuse for not having taken steps to provide new hospital accommodation early in this war, when the government must have known that large numbers of men would be brought back here for treatment. I say this because I do not think we can blame the United States people, the United States government or anyone other than our own government.
The contrast between the situation in the United States and the situation in regard to Christie Street hospital is very clearly brought out by an excerpt from the "Journal of the American Medical Association" dated October 30, 1943, and an excerpt from the Toronto

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
Telegram dated December 14, 1943, both reprinted in the News of December 18, 1943. The quotation from the United States publication is as follows:
The Schick general hospital, formally opened on October 7, is located three miles north of Clinton, Iowa. It has a capacity of 1,514 beds and 103 separate structures. The grounds consist of 89-6 acres of land. There are a chapel, laundry, post exchange, post office, ambulance service, recreational facilities and air conditioned operating rooms. Prior to the formal opening there were 2,687 patients admitted, of whom 674 were operated on. The first patient was admitted on February 15, 1943. . . . On the day of the opening there were 1,175 patients in the hospital, representing every overseas theatre of operation. The allotment of nurses is 120 and of enlisted men 512. These men are being trained as operating room, X-ray and laboratory technicians, as well as ward attendants. The project represents an investment of more than $6,000,000.
That is a report on the treatment given United States soldiers by the government of that country, fourteen months after the United States entered the war. The article reprinted from the Telegram is as follows:
Instructions have been received from Doctor R. E. Wodehouse, deputy minister of pensions and national health, ordering the whole administration staff of Christie Street hospital, numbering 165, to find other quarters at the earliest possible date, so that the hospital ground floor can be made ready for casualties returning from Sicily and Italy.
The ground floor will accommodate 140 beds, and 200 others will be placed in one-storey huts to be erected on the hospital grounds immediately.
That was four years and three months after Canada went to war. I trust that when he speaks the minister will give us an account of just what is being done at Christie street hospital to-day. Apparently it is the intention of the government to retain this hospital as a permanent institution. That is regrettable, and I am sure is not the wish of the public who are served by the hospital. I trust that the minister will tell us also what progress has been made with the new hospital that is to be built at Sunnybrook. Reference has been made already to the delay in this connection. Possibly the minister will be able to give us some good news; perhaps plans have progressed much further than would be indicated by a visit to the proposed site of the hospital. Certainly we should be pleased to hear that steps are being taken to facilitate the construction of this new institution.
I support the suggestion already made that it is time the Pension Act and the regulations under it were brought before this parliament for examination and discussion. I am confident that every hon. member of this house will agree that improvements being made now, including some which were made in the order in council brought down last week, in fairnesss
to the men who served in the last war should have been made twenty years ago. I am confident that if the regulations under that act came into this house for discussion, and hon. members were free to vote as they wished, some of those regulations would be changed. I am confident there are regulations in effect to-day which would not receive the support of a majority of hon. members of this house if they could be discussed in this chamber without hon. gentlemen opposite being required to support the government.
I have brought many cases to the attention of the minister, and I want to compliment him and his officials on the way they have been dealt with. In the three sessions I have been in this house every case I have brought before the minister or any official of his department has been given prompt attention. I have found them ready at all times to investigate cases, and in every instance where regulations permitted, some relief has been provided. I am satisfied that those who are responsible for administering the act go just as far as they possibly can, under existing regulations, to relieve injustices that exist.
But the point is that there are still regulations which in many individual cases result in injustice. I am sure there is not a member of the house who has not secured for one o-r more great war veteran an alleviation of difficulties under which he or they may have been suffering, by bringing such cases to the attention of the minister or his department. That is good; but there must be vast numbers of people whose cases are not brought before the minister or his department. I suggest it should not be necessary for great war veterans or present war veterans to have to bring their cases to the attention of members of parliament to have injustices ironed out. The machinery of the government, and of this department in particular, should be such that, not all, probably, but a great number of such cases should be handled automatically.
In this connection I wish to cite one example. A young airman, after serving 210 days, was discharged while still in hospital. Under the regulations his wife and family were allowed dependents' allowance for 210 days. Incidentally he remained in hospital for that period, and is still there. When the 210 days expired about the middle of March the allowance was cut off. The wife and two children have had no income from that time. He was cared for in the hospital. Apparently the pension board had that case under review, since the man was discharged and turned over to the Department of Pensions and National Health. On Tuesday morning of this week I received a letter in reply to one I had written the minister in which I had called his atten-
3052	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
tion to this case. His letter informed me that there was nothing the department could do for the airman in question. The regulations do not permit the granting of any allowance after the expiration of the 210 days. It was pointed out that the case was before the pension board, and that until that board reached a decision nothing could be done. I then telephoned other officials, and learned that the pension board was meeting that afternoon. Those to whom I spoke were good enough to assure me that the case in question would come before the board. The next morning I received word that after reviewing the case the board had granted the wife an allowance of $68 a month. The case is settled satisfactorily.

I believe that in time the pension board would have reviewed this case. The point is, however, that this was a man who had been discharged for nearly nine months, during the last two months of which his wife and children had received no support by way of allowances. My criticism is that that sort of thing should not be possible. There should be machinery to take care of situations of the kind. I am not taking credit for securing an adjustment in the instance to which I have referred. I have no doubt the pension board would have reviewed the case at its meeting on Tuesday afternoon. Probably it was on the agenda, and would have been dealt with. But the point is that it had stood for six months without adjustment, and apparently such adjustment did not take long, once the matter was placed before the board.
Then, there are other regulations in addition to those dealing with the granting of allowances for the length of time a man has served. There is the deduction made from allowances when a veteran is in hospital-and I presume this will apply to men in the present war. Because the hospitalization charges are high, and the government incurs considerable expense on that account, when the veteran is discharged he finds that his veteran's allowance is reduced, and several months must elapse before he catches up in his account. It seems to me the cost of hospitalization should not be calculated as a part of a man's income, under the veterans' allowance legislation.
Then, of course, there are questions connected with the ceiling on earnings. I am confident that if some of those regulations came before the house they would be revised. 
I do not think there is a member representing any constituency who would want to stand by some of the regulations.
Reference has already been made to preenlistment difficulties. I have said before, and I now repeat, that I think it is about time we accepted, for pension purposes, the medical status granted a man upon enlistment. If the doctors who examine him for the army are not able to locate those difficulties, then surely it is their fault and not that of the soldier. We must consider this whole question of taking care of the men and women who serve in the forces, and must accept the necessary expenditure as a part of tire cost of war. We are not niggardly or parsimonious when it comes to buying tanks, ships, aeroplanes or any other type of equipment needed to carry on the war. But the human wreckage caused by the war is just as much a part of the cost as is the equipment used in the prosecution of the war. I believe we must take that attitude. Certainly it is to be hoped that no one returning from this war will be required over the years to suffer the injustices that thousands of those who returned from the last war have suffered.

For a few minutes this afternoon I should like to call the minister's attention to the hospital situation in Toronto. In doing so I do not offer any criticism of the minister, because, having seen him at Christie Street hospital last November 11, Armistice day, I believe I understand his feelings in the matter.
Several returns have been made respecting the situation at Christie street hospital. During the last war I was chairman of the hospital commission which had as members the late Thomas Bradshaw and the late Doctor Hastings, that great health officer. This commission sat during the last war and for four years following. At that time the same situation existed as exists in this war. At the present time there is a scarcity of hospital accommodation all over the north American continent. I do not know where a civilian in Toronto would go to get hospital accommodation; he might die for the lack of it at the present time.
I do not want to refer to the past, because the past is gone and there is no use crying over it. During the last war I criticized the hospital accommodation provided by the government which I supported, as well as by the present government. War conditions and lack of foresight are largely to blame for the

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
existing hospital accommodation situation in Canada. A great many mistakes have been made in connection with the treatment of soldiers. During the last war we had the flu epidemic. I remember one young man who was secretary to Sir George Bury, vice president of the Canadian Pacific. He went down to the Jesse Ketchum school for a couple of days, where they had the maiming pool to enlist, and then he was moved out to a camp. He arrived on a Monday and he was dead in ten days because of the terrible flu epidemic. He was only one of many hundreds who suffered. As a result of this they looked over the Toronto district for hospital sites. One on the lake shore road was considered, where the present Goodyear tire plant is built, but it was found to be too far out. There was no Hamilton highway at that time and the city did not own the street railway or the radial line, and doctors were then only on part time. Then the plant of the Canadian Kodak building was chosen as the site of the present Christie street hospital. It was surrounded by other factories. I represented that district in three parliaments and the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Roebuck) and the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol), who has done a great deal for the soldiers in that district, know the district quite well. It was decided to use that site as temporary accommodation. There was also the old base hospital closed up and vacant on Gerrard street, the old Toronto General. Some doctor members may recall that when they were students at the university. But that was not considered fit for civilians, so that I do not see why it should have been considered for soldiers. It was used temporarily and then it was decided to go on with Christie Street. That decision was opposed by the city officials and the hospital commission, but we could not do anything about it.
In two wars the city of Toronto has been very generous to the government in turning over property free of charge, and so have the school board and the university of Toronto. There is no university in Canada that has turned over more property than the university of Toronto. But the same situation still exists. I saw a train come in the other day and I saw a number of wounded men who had come back from Italy and other places. I do not know what the minister is going to do to provide accommodation for all these people.
Two or three returns have been made about Christie Street hospital. I suggest to (he minister that he make a monthly statement as soon as possible about the progress of
Sunnybrook hospital. He has made two or three statements which were very good as far as they went. I know that hospitals are not built in a day, or in a night either. It takes weeks and years to build them. As a constructive suggestion to the government I suggest that they consider erecting some temporary buildings along the waterfront in Toronto, or in the parks or exhibition grounds, as an emergency plan until the new hospital is ready. There are other buildings at the exhibition grounds, the Stanley barracks, for instance. I passed by Stanley barracks the other day and saw a building nearly twice the size of this chamber being used as a dining room for officers in that district. I am not criticizing that at all; no doubt it is needed. The horticultural building near the fountain at the exhibition grounds is a beautiful building. The 74th and 75th battalions were housed in this building during the last war and I believe it could be temporarily converted for hospital use at very small cost.
There are a number of private schools in Toronto. In the last war they took one of these schools, St. Andrew's college in Rosedale, and made it over into a hospital. Then there is the old lacrosse grounds which was carried on something like the M.A.A. in Montreal. There are a number of properties like that which the city no doubt would be willing to give to the government. I do not know about those in Rosedale, but I know the city is ready to help in providing urgent accommodation.
Since last session the government have acquired a number of properties. There is one now acquired at Scarborough, seven miles east of the Woodbine. This is a fine property on the lake front. Then there are properties on the island; the old sick children's hospital used to used. Any number of these places could be converted and could be used for at least four or five summer months in the year, if not longer, for convalescent homes. As I say, there are sites along the harbour and lake front upon which the government has spent some money and upon which the city spent on harbour development $25,000,000 or $30,000,000. There is plenty of land available, and with the equipment and construction branches the department and the army, navy and air force have, these temporary buildings could be made very comfortable until the larger policy of modern hospitals is carried out. The Toronto East general hospital was started as a city hospital by the late Doctor Hastings. It is located in the east end of the city. A wing containing 200 rooms was taken away from civilians and given over to government use.
3054	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
No doubt it was absolutely necessary and the possibility is that the government may take over the whole building.
The duty of the government is to look after its soldiers first, but something will have to be done also for the civilians. You cannot have them out on the street Many of these people are the wives, the parents and children of soldiers overseas. The Minister of Public Works made a statement the other day about Sunnybrook. I hope there will be no delay in completing this hospital. As one who has a great deal to do with the building of public buildings I know that they are not completed over night; tenders must be called for, and all this takes time.
It is said that the completion of this hospital is held up because of the difficulty in getting equipment. The board of education in Toronto are trying to build a new wing to Riverdale collegiate as well as make additions to other collegiates and schools, including Perth Avenue in the riding of the hon. member for Davenport. The school board are trying to carry out an extensive programme but they are held up because they cannot get equipment. What is the use of talking about building houses, now castles in the air, when you cannot get the necessary building equipment? You cannot get the necessary equipment for private or public hospitals.
As I say, there are a number of private schools in Toronto as well as other properties which are exempt from taxation. Some of these could be taken over by the government and used as a means of temporarily tiding over this acute hospital situation. The necessary accommodation could be provided for soldiers and civilians alike. Something must be done immediately before the winter comes along. I do not know where we are going to be with things coming along as they are.
I think a lot has been done by the minister's department in the past six months on temporary accommodation, but there does not seem to have been much progress made on Sunnybrook. The transportation commission are willing to provide street railway services as soon as the tracks are laid. They have buses now which could go right to the door of the hospital. I have been told that the men and their families do not want to be away from the city, they want to be where proper transportation is available. The minister should inform the public monthly as to what progress is being made. I suggest that he should make a monthly report. I believe I have explained this whole situation in a fair way. The municipal services, such as light, power and transportation, can be provided immediately,
(Mr. Church.]
if the government will lead the way. The province has also offered a lot of buildings but I think that still more buildings can be used.
I had not intended to make these remarks this afternoon, but I hope that a progress report will be issued by the minister. I do hope that something further may be done to bring about in the Pension Act as in 1940, a national insurance scheme or one separate entirely from the Pension Act. I hope that when the war is over we shall not have the situation we had after the last war. This is a citizens' army of our young people overseas, and when they come back we do not want them to have to go to a commercial bank for a loan and have it refused them or have someone endorse a note for a couple of hundred dollars to enable them to start up a small grocery or a small manufacturing business of their own. The Macmillan report as I read it places this function on the Bank of Canada, I believe that the first duty and function of the Bank of Canada is to see that our soldiers when they return from the front will be able to get such credit, and I hope that provision will be made accordingly. I also trust that the minister will bring in amendments to the Pension Act embodying the constructive suggestions that have been made and that provision will also be made so that a soldier can get the small amount of capital he requires to start up in business for himself.

Mr. Chairman, I think you have been pretty generous in allowing this discussion to go far afield. I think that much of the discussion yesterday was out of order.
I want to associate myself with one or two of the many constructive suggestions that have been made. I refer particularly to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Vancouver South that the minister bring in amendments to the Pension Act so that the onus will not be on the returned man to make application for pension but rather on the government to prove that the man is not eligible for pension. The status of a man before his enlistment is also worthy of consideration.
A good deal has been said with regard to hospitals and hospitalization. We have heard about Christie Street hospital almost every day, and if there is any way of settling that problem to the satisfaction of some of the Toronto members I do hope that the minister will do it. The hon. member for Melfort suggested decentralization of hospitals and hospital services. I think that that too is worthy of consideration, so that when the men return they may be able to secure hospitalization in the part of the country from which they came. I think that would be well

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
worth while. Suggestions were made as to where certain health centres should be located. I am never backward in making suggestions to the minister with respect to my own bailiwick or my own part of the country. Might I remind him that at Fort Qu'Appelle there is one of the finest sanatoria in western Canada, and it is doing splendid work. It is second to none, I was going to say, in Canada. A convalescent home in the Fort Qu'Appelle district for men who do not require complete hospitalization but rather a rest home would be ideally located.
I am sure we are all anxious to do everything in our power for the returned men and appreciate our responsibility to them. I agree entirely with what the hon. member for Edmonton East said this afternoon when she spoke of the responsibility of the people at home. I think we all realize what the men will expect of us when they do return home.
I received just to-day a letter from a doctor who has been overseas four years. I shall not read it, but I wish some of the members would read this letter because it shows what is taking place in the minds of the men overseas. He says that the men hardly know what is going on in Canada now because they have been away from their homes and families for so long and have been doing nothing but training and getting ready to fight. He said that some of them were not very much concerned about Canada now, that all they were interested in is fighting and winning this war. This letter goes to prove that the men will come back in a very different frame of mind. He said that they are most interested in meeting men who have come back to Canada and then returned overseas, but he says that after hearing the story of these men they seem to be more confused than ever because of the reports they bring about the conditions back home.
The minister will recall that when the estimates of the Minister of Labour were before the committee I brought up the question of training ex-service men in schools and getting them prepared to start up in business for themselves. I trust that these schools will be continued, although some have not been successful, and some were started with a misunderstanding. I see the minister is smiling a little, but there was certainly a misunderstanding on the part of the men attending one school, as I think the minister was quite willing to admit. I think he is willing to see that justice is done to these men. It is a splendid thing to establish these schools where men can fit themselves for entering a new line of business. Many of our men went overseas when they were still young and had 100-192
never been in business. It will be difficult for them when they come back to decide what line of business they want to follow.
I am pleased to note that some of the suggestions that have been made by the members of the opposition within the last two or three years have been implemented in amendments to the Pension Act. I am glad that the minister has seen the merit of those suggestions.
I do not want to rehash what was said yesterday. The hon. member for Trinity, referring to the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough, said that he was just threshing old straw. Personally I do not think the hon. member for Trinity would know straw if he saw it. I think the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough made a most constructive speech and I hope that many of his suggestions will receive the consideration of the minister and be implemented, even though they may not have carried much weight with the hon. member for Trinity.
I said, Mr. Chairman, that I was going to take only five minutes, and my time has almost expired. I think a man can say as much in five or ten minutes as some say in forty minutes. We all want to get on with the business of the house, so that I shall say mo more.

Mr. Chairman, I too
shall follow the good example set this afternoon and speak very briefly. I come from a riding with more enlistments both in *the last war and this than any other riding in Canada, I was going to say, but I will say more than any other riding that I know of. The riding is settled pretty largely by old country folks who have enlisted in great numbers in this war, as they did in the last. During the last fifteen years I have had a great deal to do with bringing to the attention of the department the troubles of many returned soldiers, and I am happy to say as regards the vast majority of cases I have no complaint as to the way they were finally .treated. I did _pot get all I tried to get, or all that the men for whom I was speaking asked for, but in the great majority of cases relief was given. So that I cannot, so far as my own experience goes, find too much fault with the department. In the course of these years I have noted some points which might be considered with benefit by the department in looking after the soldiers coming back from the present war.
A number of the cases with which I was concerned had to do with soldiers who were captured and held in prison camps in Ger-

3056	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
many. I suggest that the department should make every effort, of course through neutral sources, to get particulars as to the treatment of our prisoners in German camps and the effect upon them of the conditions there, and that they should make similar observations of their own concerning German soldiers in prison camps in Canada, so that the effects of prison life on soldiers may be more exactly determined. I have had to deal with many men who were, and in my judgment are yet, suffering from prison camp life in Germany. Undoubtedly the food was not what it should have been, and coupled with it, the fear of being shot, the desire to escape, all the unpleasant elements of prison life in the last war, could not fail to have had their effects. I hope the department will make a special effort in the way of ascertaining the effects of imprisonment upon the health of soldiers who are prisoners of war.
A great number of people whose physical condition was far from perfect have enlisted in this war. In many cases I took the trouble, even prior to their enlistment, to write to the authorities advising them that this man had very flat feet, that that man was subject to bronchitis, or one thing and the other, yet these men were enlisted and classed A-l. I can never understand how a man with a disability which even the ordinary layman can see and understand can be enlisted as A-l. After serving in the army for a year or more a number have been discharged. I wonder what is their position if, having been classed as A-l, they apply for a pension. The department will have records of the particular cases which I have had to deal with, and doubtless many more, and I assume that these records will be held up to these boys if they apply for pension. There is a great deal in the contention which has already been made that anyone who passes a medical investigation one hundred per cent should become the responsibility of the government, unless, of course, he subsequently commits some misdemeanour which disentitles him to consideration.
Everyone has had something to do with soldiers who, coming back physically fit or apparently fit, have refused to apply for a pension and have later become ill. Many men with whom I am well acquainted fell sick as a consequence,_ they claimed, of war disabilities, but not having applied for or accepted a pension they were refused admission to military hospital. I think a change for the better could be made there. Any man who served in France during the last war or has been on active service in this war, if he

is discharged as one hundred per cent fit, should not be denied consideration if he later becomes ill and is not on pension. I do not believe there is a doctor living who can state positively and prove that a man upon discharge is one hundred per cent fit. If what I suggest is not in accordance with the act, there should be an amendment which will permit treatment of men of the class I have mentioned. I know many who fought in the trenches three or four years, who did not receive a pension when they returned, and who later, when ill, were refused admittance to a military hospital.
Another class of returned soldier with whom I have had a good deal to do is the imperial. In my part of Toronto, and no doubt in Victoria and Vancouver, where so many imperial soldiers went, there are many who saw long service in the British army and served during the whole of the last war. I have in -mind a man who saw service in Turkey, at the Dardanelles, in Egypt and in India. Now, having taken ill out here, he cannot go to a military hospital, nor can he obtain a pension. I believe this has been mentioned by another hon. member, and I would add my plea that the department try its best to make some reciprocal arrangement with the British government, in order that imperial soldiers who have been out here five, ten, fifteen or twenty years shall be entitled to consideration in respect of pensions and hospitalization.
I am not going to say anything critical of Christie street hospital. Other Toronto members have spoken on the subject and I can add nothing to what they have said. I know that lately some improvements have been made, and I would suggest a further one- not with the intention that the government should continue to operate the place, but as they are going to keep it for a while there is no reason why they should not improve it. The elevator service is bad, as I know because of the frequent trips I make to visit people from my riding. It is just east of my constituency; in fact it is in a riding which at one time I represented. The government should put in escalators which would go at least from the ground floor to the first floor, where half the patients are located. I have seen elevators crowded repeatedly with the relatives and friends of patients. It would be much easier for visitors and it would not cost much to install an electric escalator so that people could go from one floor to the other without the inconvenience which they experience now.

Just before he went away he told me that the department had been very good in taking off the hospital's hands a new wing of 200 rooms, so that there is another mark in the department's favour.
As regards Sunnybrook, after all that has been said about it, the only thing I can suggest is that the contracts be called as speedily as possible and, the work undertaken with the greatest rapidity humanly possible. If there are cases in Christie street hospital that are not in danger of dying, but that require only daily or weekly medical attention, it would be nice if they could be moved to Toronto island in the summer and brought back in the fall. There is no finer place in the world than Toronto island. It would cost little, if buildings are not available, to put up suitable tents. The military department has ample tents, because if there were a great fire in Montreal or Halifax or Hamilton or anywhere else they would quickly find the tents. That is one place where summer comfort could be given to patients in Christie Street hospital.
Recently I had to do with a soldier returning from the present war. He had been in many actions, had been under fire and had been wounded. He was not discharged at the time I met him but was home. He was away without leave on several different occasions and as a matter of fact when I went to see him he was in the clink. While in the clink he told me he felt he had been ill-treated. He had been through a great deal, and the very place that he had served in, Dunkirk, was enough to throw anyone's nerves off colour.

I hope every effort will be made to give these boys who are coming back from such terrible and bloody experience the most considerate and sympathetic treatment possible, and if they commit a few misdemeanours there should be some other way of dealing with them than by putting them in the clink. At any rate, I would be chary of putting these boys in the clink, for they have offered themselves as a human sacrifice on our behalf.
Lastly, I hope that those who are returning from this war will be more frequently accorded the consideration intended by this House of Commons when it wrote into the present act that the soldier should be given the benefit of the doubt. That the presumption should be established that a man's condition as recorded on his admission to the service was in fact his condition at that time; and that any subsequent deterioration in his condition was due to his service. In putting these clauses on the record I desire to associate those members of our party who have not spoken with the claim that is put forward in this programme.
In closing, I should like to impress this consideration upon the minister with regard to changes in the law, if one may put it in that way, which have been brought down by the minister in recent times. I suggest to

I think he will agree that the debate has been productive of many worth-while suggestions; and I hope that in consequence, from time to time, the government will be enabled to do a better job for that branch of our citizens who are entitled to have a better job done for them than any other section of the Canadian people.

Before I come to deal briefly with some of the questions which were brought up in the course of the discussion with regard to pensions, treatment and rehabilitation, I wish to say a word about the suggestions made yesterday by some hon. members in regard to matters

affecting the national health. The hon. member for Parkdale, the hon. member for Renfrew South, the hon. member for Portneuf and the hon. member for Medicine Hat all made what I consider valuable contributions in connection with this question. Emphasis was placed by the hon. member for Parkdale on the national menace in regard to venereal disease, and the hon. member for Renfrew South was able to point out that recently we had a national campaign, wThich I trust may have most fruitful results, to deal with this menace. The necessity of watching cases on discharge, in connection with this disease, was mentioned by the hon. member for Portneuf. I agree with the hon. member for Parkdale as to the wonderfully valuable service rendered to Canada by Colonel Williams, who happened to do his pioneering work in British Columbia. He did wonderful work for that province; since then he has done wonderful work for the dominion, and he is now becoming an international authority on this question, so that my fear is that he may be taken from us for service in larger spheres. The hon. member for Medicine Hat mentioned a recent typhoid epidemic in the west, and I can assure him that as far as the powers of the Department of Pensions and National Health go w7e shall pay very great heed to the suggestions he made yesterday.
The hon. member for Portneuf referred to the question of psychoneurosis, and mentioned one case by number. He rather conveyed the impression, if I followed him correctly, that there was a rigid bar against pensionability in cases of neurosis. I wish immediately to assure him and the committee that there is no such bar and that there never will be; that unless there is positive proof, as a result of the history of the case, that the psychoneurosis was a preenlistment condition, anyone suffering from the stresses and strains of battle would be pensionable, and that this would be the policy followed by the Canadian pension commission. I have reviewed the case to which he made reference, and without mentioning the name I find that following service in Canada and England this man was discharged on January 24, 1941, as medically unfit for further service because of anxiety neurosis. He was married, with seven dependent children. The record shows that in September, 1940, when hospitalized in England he gave a history of headaches, choking feelings and anxiety symptoms for the past seven years. He stated that the last time he felt really well was seven years ago, when a doctor told him that there was nothing serious but that he oould not do anything for him. He was returned to Canada and admitted to
Ste. Anne's hospital, where he stated that he had always been jumpy, high-strung and worried easily. Following treatment at Ste. Anne's he claimed that he was much improved and that he was practically as well as on enlistment. From a physical point of view he was reported as perfectly normal and treatment was terminated on February 7, 1941. The pension commission has ruled on first and second hearings that anxiety neurosis was preenlistment and not aggravated. When notified of the second hearing ruling on February 20, 1942, he was advised of his right to request a hearing before an appeal board of the commission. Since that time there has been no further correspondence. That may have been a very difficult case, but I wish to emphasize this, because it is most important that the impression should not go out that there is a rigid or an automatic bar against recognition of the pensionability of these neurosis cases.
During the course < f the debate another suggestion was made by the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough and this afternoon by the hon. member for York South. In the course of their remarks they said something which I rather regretted-I will not say resented-when they called the hospital at Toronto a national disgrace. Well, Mr. Chairman, that is not a fact; it is not correct. We are now building, as hon. members know, probably the finest hospital in the dominion, but in Christie Street hospital will be found one of the ablest staffs, doctors and nurses and administrative staff, to be found anywhere in Canada. The strange thing is that patients who have been there, if they have a repetition of their disabilities, all want to go back *to the same hospital. That is well known in the department. I know the situation is not ideal; I recognize that the location is not perfect, but this was a legacy which I inherited when I took up my duties in this department. We are now improving it; we have improved it very much this last year, and we are improving it still more, because in the ordinary course of events the new hospital cannot be ready for some time yet, and Christie Street will see us over the peak. There is no intention whatever of continuing it as a permanent institution, as some hon. gentleman mentioned this afternoon.
There has been some suggestion of delay, and some good friends of mine made facetious reference to the turning of the sod last Armistice day. The question of policy with regard to providing new hospitalization in Toronto for returning casualties involved a finely balanced decision. There were two schools of thought. The first was that temporary accommodation in the vicinity of the established Christie Street hospital should be provided, wdiere new patients would have the benefit of the complete hospital service and equipment developed at that centre. The other school of thought believed that we should have a completely modern, new hospital on a more advantageous site. Each of these policies had its disadvantages. By 'the first we would have been investing further large sums in an admittedly unsuitable institution. By the second we incurred the risk of delay; for a new institution, equipped in all points, necessarily takes longer to provide and there was no point in establishing it in temporary huts or on a temporary basis. The second alternative had overwhelming public support, and has been adopted. Pending the development of these new facilities we have acquired the use of 200 beds in the East Toronto hospital, and we have removed a number of older veterans requiring permanent institutional care to the former Oddfellows home near Christie Street, now known as the Red Chevron, to which the hon. member for Davenport just made reference. In connection with the accommodation being provided by the East Toronto hospital I wish to express my appreciation of the cooperation of the hon. member for Dan-forth, who is now overseas.
Whatever may be said about the site and suitability of the Christie Street hospital buildings, that hospital is equipped with the most complete facilities for all-round clinical services to the sick and wounded members of our forces, and is served by the cream of the medical profession of the city of Toronto.

Having accepted the disadvantage of loss of time in getting the new hospital ready we have renovated and greatly improved the accommodation at Christie Street hospital, which must continue in use until the move into the new hospital can be made. One of the improvements is an increased provision of private and semi-private accommodation for seriously ill and post-operative cases. I think the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough referred to that yesterday.

I am referring to this letter because it happened to reach me this morning. But I am happy to say that many such letters testify to the quality of service rendered by the staff in our departmental hospitals.
This letter reads as follows:
My son has just returned to his home after a three-week stay in Philadelphia with relatives, to get some sunshine after four months in military hospitals.
May I express to you, sir, my appreciation of the way in which he was treated in the Camp Hill hospital, Halifax, the Christie Street hospital, Toronto, and in the manner in which his case was treated, under the regulations with regard to discharges.

I now wish to deal briefly with a question which has been mentioned by several hon. members, namely the insurance principle. I am now going to retrace the history of what has occurred in each country, so that every hon. member may be quite familiar with it. I wish to have on the record the situation all across the empire with respect to this insurance principle.
To take first the United Kingdom: Under amendments to the royal warrant passed in August, 1943, disability or death is accepted as due to war service if it is certified that
(a)	the disability is due to a wound, injury or disease which (i) is attributable to war services or (ii) existed before or arose during war service and has been and remains aggravated thereby; or (b) the death was due to or hastened by (i) a wound, injury or disease which was attributable to war service or (ii) the aggravation by war service of a wound, injury or disease which existed before or arose during war service.
No onus of proof is now on the claimant and the benefit of any reasonable doubt is given him. This is subsequent to what was mentioned yesterday by one hon. member. It will be seen, therefore, that while the insurance principle is technically not in effect for Great Britain, the provisions governing entitlement have been considerably broadened in favour of the applicant.
Then, with respect to the United States: The underlying principle would seem to be "line of duty" with modifications. The insurance principle does not apply there.
Then, for Australia: Disability or death must be directly attributable to having sustained a war injury. Special provision is made for tuberculosis. The insurance principle is not in force.
For New Zealand:	Provisions closely
resemble those of Canada. Pension is payable for death or disablement while on service overseas, or nevertheless attributable or aggravated by such service. When service has been in New Zealand only, the death or disablement must be actually due to service with the forces. Accidents or injuries while on leave are not pensionable. The insurance principle is not in force.
For South Africa: The insurance principle is not in force.
So that, after reviewing every single country of the commonwealth and the United States, the insurance principle as we have been advocating it here, and as we had it in Canada for the great war, is not to-day in force in any of these countries. I am not saying that because of that I am opposed to the insurance principle. It was discontinued because it was
found that certain abuses arose early in 1940, abuses which were most regrettable. A change was made at that time, and the order in council of May 21, 1940 was adopted.
Then, as was stated by the hon. member for Vancouver South, this subject was most carefully reviewed before the committee on the Pension Act which sat in 1941. The present section 11(3) was placed in the act to meet needy cases, and has been most effective, in a commendable way. Although it is not equal to full recognition of the Pension Act, it has been most effective in solving questions which could not otherwise be met.
