I shall now discuss the question of decentralization-and I am taking these points as rapidly as I can. This question was discussed by several hon. members during the course of the debate. Staff shortages were mentioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre last night. These two subjects can best be considered together. On account of the war we live in a time of shortages of man-power and of commodities of all kinds. Because of these shortages we have to make the greatest possible use of what is available. That is one of the reasons why it has been necessary to concentrate hospital services for members and ex-members of the forces in a comparatively small number of large hospitals. Another reason is that in large centres of population there are assembled groups of leading specialists in all branches of medical science. We employ these specialists on part-time salary.
As a result of having our hospitals close to large centres of population we are able to obtain for sick and disabled veterans the services of the leading specialists in Canada as and when they are needed. This would be much more difficult in a large number of widely scattered small hospitals. By centralization we raise the standard of medical services. The same consideration applies to the infinite variety of specialized hospital equipment. In times of scarcity it would be wasteful and probably impracticable to attempt to set up thirty or forty fully equipped small hospitals or hospital units. But in the small number of hospitals that we have it is possible to install complete equipment.	.
With respect to the staff problem we have experienced definite shortages, and our officials and employees in many cases have to do more work than we would ordinarily ask of them in normal times. The Department of Pensions and National Health is short in its

medical establishment by seventy-three doctors, according to what I am told by our advisers. The situation, however, is not quite as bad as would have appeared from the figures correctly quoted by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. The number of patient-days shown in the return from which he quoted includes the patients in approximately 1,320 beds in pensions department hospitals, which beds have been temporarily allocated to the armed services. These patients receive their medical attendance from service medical officers. These navy, army and air force medical officers who are in our hospitals attending to the service patients cooperate with the medical officers of my department by serving other patients who are on our own charge. The extent of this service cannot be stated statistically, but it is of material assistance.
Over and above that measure of cooperation, the armed services have placed additional medical officers at the disposal of the Department of Pensions and National Health, In numbers that vary from month to month. It is not possible to state exactly the number of service doctors thus giving full time to the department, but I am advised that thirty-seven would be a good estimate. In Camp Hill, where the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre pointed out that the number of doctors on the pensions and national health staff is actually less than it was in 1939, we have the full-time services of not less than five or six service medical officers. In Toronto this number is not less than fifteen.
The deficiency in our own staff is, therefore, largely made up by these two factors: first, the part-time services of medical officers assigned to care for service patients in pensions department hospitals and, second, the full-time services of approximately thirtv-seven service medical officers assigned to duK in pensions hospitals.
Further steps are being taken to meet the shortage of doctors by advertising positions at higher salaries than have hitherto prevailed. Yesterday the hon. member for Renfrew South spoke about the low remuneration paid to these doctors, but I may say that we now have authority to offer as high as 86,500 a year to certain types of specialists. In addition, we have been advised of the possibility that some of the older medical officers with considerable periods of service overseas may shortly be replaced by younger men in the services, and thus made available for the care of patients returned to Canada and in our hospitals.
The question of private nurses was raised by the hon. member for Hastings-Peterbor-

ough. Private nurses are assigned to seriously ili and post-operative cases whenever the medical officer considers it is necessary. When it is possible, nurses are selected from the hospital permanent staff, but when these are not available application is made to the nurses' registry. I come now to a discussion of the question which was brought up, I think, by most of those who spoke yesterday, namely, the recent changes in the British regulations affecting entitlement. Several hon. gentlemen placed upon the record parts of a statement made by Sir John Anderson in London when the debate was on. The hon. member for Vancouver South read the first two paragraphs dealing with entitlement, but he overlooked the third paragraph which is vital and which relates more directly to preenlistment or A-l condition than the other two. This is from the ministry of pensions, "Changes in War Pensions", page 2, paragraph 4:
There remains to be considered the claim, "Fit for Service, Fit for Pension." This claim is inconsistent with the principle, which obtained in regard to the war of 1914-18 and has since been maintained, that there must be a causal connection between disablement and war service to enable a pension to be awarded. H.M. government reaffirms this principle and is accordingly unable to accept the claim, "Fit for Service, Fit for Pension." Its acceptance would mean that the minister of pensions would assume liability for a condition which became manifest at any time after the commencement of war service whether or not service had played a part in its onset or development. In the view of H.M. government a disablement in which war service has played no part should be dealt with under the ordinary social service provisions.
Although they have certainly broadened the provisions, according to the paragraphs mentioned yesterday by my hon. friend, they are far from admitting the claims "Fit for Service, Fit for Pension."
The minister must not misunderstand me; I did not advocate that.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
No; it was done by another speaker. Preenlistment origin is one of the most widely discussed questions in this debate. No discharged man is denied pension on the ground that his disability was of preenlistment origin unless there is positive evidence that that is the case. In many cases brought to my personal attention, I have found, upon inquiry from the commission, that the man has himself quite frankly stated that he had suffered injury or illness of the type in question prior to 100-193
joining up. In other cases, precise hospital records have been brought to the commission's attention. There is no class of case, I am advised, in which the commission is more disposed to give the applicant the benefit of the doubt, and entitlement is denied only where the evidence is positive.
Much has been said about the careful examination given at time of enlistment. I am advised that, without disclosure of facts, no medical man can guarantee accurate diagnosis. In the medical examination at the time of enlistment, the medical man has to rely upon what can be observed by the various tests which are used and upon information from the recruit. If he withholds information or does not give truthful information, the medical officers may be misled. We all realize that it is not to a man's discredit if, in his anxiety to be of service, he refrains from disclosing some previous illness, the disclosure of which might debar him from service. It does not follow, from the view we may take of this action on the part of the recruit, that the country should undertake to provide pension for a disability which did not arise out of or even during military service.
I now wish to deal with the question raised by the hon. member for Vancouver South, that of accidents. Yesterday the hon. member referred to a statement by Sir John Anderson in the British House of Commons dealing with the policy of the British ministry of pensions as related to accidents sustained by members of the forces. Briefly, the statement was to the effect that His Majesty's government has decided that under war conditions accidents sustained, (a) whilst "walking out" in spare time; (b) whilst travelling to and from home on short pass; (c) whilst travelling to and from duty when living in accommodation privately arranged, can reasonably be regarded as attributable to service. The fourth category was accidents sustained whilst actually on leave.
In the latter cases His Majesty's government consider "the compulsions of service play no part and an accident sustained in such circumstances cannot properly be regarded as attributable to service". The Canadian pension commission advises me that with regard to members of the forces serving in Great Britain or anywhere beyond Canada the provisions of the Pension Act are more generous and provide full protection under section 11, subsection 1, of the act with respect to all such accidents. That is, accidents outside Canada.
The British cover all accidents outside Great Britain.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
The Pension Act provides two principles for

3064	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
dealing with disabilities which arise out of accidents to members of the forces in Canada.
(1)	In respect of military service, during the war with the German reich, any part of which has been rendered outside of Canada, the Pension Act provides full insurance coverage for everything that happened during that man's service. If he is involved in an accident, compensation is paid for death or disability resulting from that accident and there need be no direct service causation of the condition. He is fully protected in regard to any disability which may result from an accident unless he was on leave of absence without pay at the time the accident took place-
Is that in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I am speaking of men who have served outside Canada-or unless, during his leave of absence with pay, undertaken an occupation which was unconnected with military service and the accident had arisen during the course of that occupation.
(2)	In respect of military service which has been wholly rendered in Canada pension is awarded for disability or death resulting from an accident when the accident arose out of or was directly connected with military service.
The other clause had reference to service rendered partly in and partly out of Canada.
That is the difference.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
While not providing full insurance coverage for all accidents that happen in Canada to members of the forces whose service is restricted to Canada only, this principle has a very broad application. While somewhat analogous to the conditions of workmen's compensation, the Canadian pension commission gives it a much broader application than the provincial workmen's compensation act and also a wider application than the United States phrase " in line of duty." It is not necessary that the injury should have been caused by some incident or occurrence peculiar only to the performance of military duty such as the discharge of a weapon or an accident while driving a military vehicle, but rather that the man should have been in the course of his service exposed to a hazard related to that service. For instance, any person engaged in games designed to improve the physique as a part of the training is entitled as of right to pension consideration for any injury so incurred.
The question of leave has been given careful consideration. A man returning from leave by an ordinary, legitimate method of transportation who suffers a fortuitous accident is undoubtedly entitled to pension consideration for

any disability resulting therefrom, as is a man who is on living-out pass who suffers a similar accident going to and from his duty from his place of dwelling by proper means. Such cases have received favourable ruling from the pension commission.
A striking example is the Almonte train wreck, in which favourable consideration as of right was given to all members of the services who were killed or injured in that accident.
Another type of case is one in which the commission recognized death by drowning where the man, although not on a regular ordered bathing parade, was bathing with a group of comrades at a place which was allotted for such purpose and to which the men were encouraged to go during the warm weather when they were not on parade. It will be observed that the basis of entitlement under this section is that the accident must have arisen out of or been directly connected with the man's military service. Each case is decided on its own merits after careful inquiry. When an accident occurs, the military authorities hold a court of inquiry, and when the man is discharged from the forces, a copy of the evidence before this court of inquiry is supplied to the pension commission and the commission decision is reached only after a careful study of all the evidence adduced at the hearing.
It is the policy of the commission to award entitlement as of right in all cases of accidents where service was a factor.
It must always be remembered, however, that an unfavourable decision under section 11 (2) does not exhaust the benefits of the Pension Act. Where a disability results from an accident which is not considered to have arisen out of or been directly connected with military service, an award of pension is made if the applicant is seriously disabled and in necessitous circumstances.
That is only under a means test?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes. This question is one of very great difficulty. The difficulty is this, that the War Veterans Allowance Act in Canada has been applied only to those who saw service in the main in a theatre of actual war, and Canadians who served in Canada and in England in the great war are not eligible, excepting in a small number of cases, for the benefits of the act. If it is decided by this house or by any government to give entitlement to veterans' allowances to imperial soldiers who fought in the great war, the same right cannot consistently be denied to Canadians who went overseas from Canada. That is the difficulty all through the years. If it should ever come about that the veterans' allowance act were broadened out to cover Canadians who served in England only, the difficulty would largely vanish.
The unfortunate part of that matter is that the imperial authorities have turned down flat the vast majority of imperial soldier applicants. They give them no consideration.

For pensions.

[Mr. Ian Mackenzie.!

speechtext: Not by the Canadian government; by the British government.

speechtext: I happen to have been born in the old country, and I say it would be distinctly unfair to grant the allowance to imperial veterans who served in a theatre of war and not to Canadians who went overseas but were not allowed to serve in a theatre of war.

The minister did not make
the position quite clear with regard to the question of presumptions. I wish he would correct me if I am wrong as I make my statement. As I understand it, the position in Great Britain since last summer is this: they now have in their royal warrant under which pensions can be granted this provision; it is paragraph (3), which will be found near the top of page 3 in the white paper to which both the minister and myself have referred:
(3) Where an injury or disease which has led to a member's discharge or death during war service was not noted in a medical report made on that member on the commencement of his war service, a certificate under paragraph (1) shall be given unless the evidence shows that the conditions set out in that paragraph are not fulfilled.

W'ar Appropriation-Pensions and Health
The white paper on page 1 explains just what those presumptions mean, in these words:
His .Majesty's government accepts the view that the fact that a man is accepted for service in the present war in a cetrain medical category may be taken as presumptive evidence that (a) at the time of acceptance he was fit for the kind of service demanded of a man in that medical category; and (to) in the event of his toeing subsequently discharged on medical grounds any deterioration in his health which has taken place is due to his service.
I suggest to the minister and the committee that we have no provision of that type in our Canadian pension law. We have no provision which goes that far. It is operative now in Great Britain; I believe it is necessary-under the conditions which have arisen in the present war, and I would urge upon the minister and the committee to see to it that Canada adopts those presumptions. They will help the disabled man to get a fair deal, and make it just that much easier for him to qualify for pension, and I think they are absolutely fair.
Mr. STIRLING; And they are exactly what we are asking for here.

And as the hon. member for Yale points out, they are exactly what we have advocated in the policy of the Progressive Conservative party. Quite apart from whether this party or any other party advocates it, it is a fair provision. I think the minister will admit that we have no such provision in the present Pension Act; it could very well be added to section 62 of the .act, which is what we call the benefit-of-the-doubt section. The British also have a benefit-of-the-doubt section, but they go that one step further and establish those two presumptions in favour of the men, and I think it is the sense of the members of this house and of the people of Canada that there should be that change here. I thought Sir John Anderson put the general attitude of the people of Great Britain and the attitude which should be adopted by this house clearly when, on July 20, 1943, he used these words, found on page 717 of the British Hansard:
The treatment to be meted out to those who have made sacrifices for their country, who have lost their lives maybe, leaving dependents, or . who come back shattered by wounds or disease, is a matter which engages the public conscience, and we should not rest content with any solution whioh fails to command the support of the overwhelming mass of reasonable people.
At the present time the Canadian Pension Act does not go far enough in this respect, and I urge upon the minister that he have steps taken to amend the pension law so that those two presumptions become part of the
charter of the men who will be returning from the various fronts. Will the minister admit that we have no such provision in the Canadian Pension Act at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: In regard to the benefit of the doubt, we are about on a par now with Great Britain. In regard to the presumption mentioned by my hon. friend in the paragraph dealing with entitlement, my interpretation and my officers' interpretation of this is that the word "deterioration" here is equivalent to the provision we have had in the Canadian Pension Act with regard to aggravation. That is, we pension for the aggravation of a disability where the disability becomes increased on active service. But I would be glad to look carefully into the interpretation, and if my interpretation is not correct I shall have the matter carefully examined and see what can be done.

I think the minister's advisers are quite wrong in that interpretation. They say that the word "deterioration" refers to an aggravation of a condition that existed before enlistment. If the minister will read the debate in the British house he will see that that was not the intention. Sir John Anderson said, at page 718:
The first presumption-I am putting this in non-technical language-is that a man's condition as recorded on his admission to the service was in fact his condition at that time. The second is that any subsequent deterioration . . .
In other words, if the man enlisted as fit. That is the type of case to which I referred.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is aggravation.

To continue the quotation:
The second is that any subsequent deterioration in his condition was due to his service.
The minister's advisers have given him the wrong advice in regard to the interpretation of the British act, and I suggest that he should have the matter reviewed again and use his own judgment.
The other question to which I wish to refer is the . insurance principle. In that regard, again, it is the sense of the members of this house that there should at least be a return to the insurance principle so far as some of the men serving in Canada are concerned. There is not a member who has spoken against it; not one has said a word in opposition to it. Of course, the position is this. There are in Canada many men in training who have enlisted for service anywhere. They are kept here because those are the orders of the army, the navy, or the air force, as the case may be. I suggest that those men who, in

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
the eyes of the general public, are ready to serve anywhere should be covered by the insurance principle. Perhaps it should not be extended to cover men not willing to serve anywhere, but it certainly should be extended to cover these other men I have mentioned. Section 11 (3), to which the minister referred, is really a stop-gap. He has admitted that it was brought in because we disagreed in the special committee that dealt with pensions in 1941. One or two of us thought the insurance principle covering all men in our forces should be left in the act, but we were voted down by the rest of the committee, and as a final solution-it was not a compromise because we never agreed to it-this provision 11 (3) was brought in. But it contains the means test. A man can get pension only if he is very hard up. He can get that pension only if he has a serious disability as distinguished from one that might not be considered serious, and he is entirely in the hands of the commission. If they had a good breakfast this morning they may give him a pension; if they have a poor breakfast to-morrow mom ing and do not feel so well they can turn down his application. I do not say that they do this, but there is too much discretion given to the commission in such cases. There should not be a large number of cases handled under a discretionary section of this type. The man should have the right to get his pension instead of having to depend on the discretion of these commissioners-at least, where he is willing to serve anywhere and suffers his disability before he has been able to get out of the country.
The minister said that they have not the insurance principle in Great Britain. There again I think he is wrong. His advisers have given him bad advice, because in effect the insurance principle does exist in Great Britain. If the minister will read the debate in the British House of Commons he will find that Sir John Anderson is reported to have said at page 723:
When soldiers are on foreign service their whole conditions of life will be covered.
That is in effect the insurance principle.
It is only when they return temporarily to the ordinary conditions of their civil life-as when a man goes normally on leave to his home in this country-that they will not be covered. That is the one exception.
Yesterday I read Sir John Anderson's further explanation in which he said, as reported at page 722:
We are giving the fullest possible application of the doctrine that a service man places himself wholly and unreservedly at the disposal of the state during his service and we are covering everything with one exception.

The exception was illustrated by the case where a man at home fell off a ladder.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: They are all theatres of actual war there, which is our definition.

That is not the British test. They do not put it on that ground. They say that once a man has given his life to the service he is under the control of the service and should be covered, except when he is home on leave. The Minister of Pensions, Sir Walter Womersley, at page 798, said:
The only case which does not come within that ruling is when a man is spending his leave at home, or with friends, or going about just like any other civilian, or doing some occupation which very often cannot be described as having anything to do with military service. The government feel that they cannot go to that extreme and that the man must come into the ordinary social services for compensation.
That shows how far they are going, and I use the accident cases only by way of illustration. I think there are far more hardship cases in connection with disability, where a man is ill. Where a man, in the service in Canada becomes ill and is discharged it is almost impossible for him to get a pension. I do not know what the figures are up to the present time. It was incurred during service, but not directly attributable to his service. That situation I suggest to the minister is unfair.

I was very much impressed by the stand taken by the president of the Canadian Legion with regard to the question of the insurance principle. I refer, of course, to Mr. Alex. Walker, who, I think, has been a splendid president of the legion, and has rendered great service to the returned men of Canada. I hold in my hand a copy of the Legionary, the official publication of the Canadian Legion. This is the issue for December, 1942, and contains a statement by Mr. Walker from which I propose to read. It is headed, "Repudiated Pledge," and states:
At the outbreak of the present war the government pledged itself to apply all the benefits of the existing Pension Act, including the insurance principle to those enlisted for active

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
service. A special order in council was passed under the War Measures Act giving effect to this pledge. However on May 21, 1940, the government changed their policy, repudiated their .pledge I say, and definitely excluded all those whose service was in Canada only from the benefits of the insurance principle in a new order in council. The Canadian Legion immediately registered strong objections, and the government announced that a special committee of the House of Commons would be appointed later to go into the matter.
Mr. Walker goes on to explain about the sittings of the special committee in 1941, about the representations made to the committee by the legion, and finally about some relief being granted by section 11 (3). Then he says this:
Two and one-half years of experience has shown the many grave injustices done to men who have contracted diseases which it is impossible to demonstrate "arose out of, and were directly connected with military service." Yet many of these men have served along our coasts, exposed to all kinds of weather, and there must always be grave doubt as to the effect of such service.
Is the government willing to take any steps to review this whole question of the insurance principle, as it applies to the men who have served only in Canada? Will the minister give any hope that this question will be considered again?	,

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: My hon. friend has asked a question regarding government policy, which I cannot answer. But I can assure him that the insurance principle, and every other question connected with the Pension Act are being reviewed from week to week and from month to month, constantly. No doubt this question will be reviewed again, as it has been in the past.

There are one or two other questions which I asked the minister yesterday, but which he did not answer to-day. One had to do with soldiers being discharged from the anny to the Department of Pensions and National Health. I asked yesterday why it was not possible for a soldier to be treated as a soldier right through until he is discharged to civil life, or until his medical rehabilitation has been completed, rather than be considered first as a charge of the army, and then, when he becomes ill or disabled, a charge of the Department of Pensions and National Health. I believe that in some cases that change means that the soldier receives less pay, or that his dependents receive less. Why is it not possible to have him treated as a soldier, receiving the pay and allowances of a soldier, until he is discharged to civilian life? The minister did not deal with that matter.
He also said nothing about the complaint made against making changes in the Pension Act by order in council, rather than by amendments to the act. I refer to changes announced just two or three days ago.
Then, he sad nothing about the veterans' guard. He will remember I pointed out yesterday that these men are now reaching the ages of fifty-five or sixty years. Those who are discharged as fit will have great difficulty in securing jobs. My suggestion was that some provision should be made for a service pension. They have served this country in two wars, and some of them will have served for periods of eight, or nine, or even ten years. It would be unfair to force them to take a war veterans allowance, and certainly it would be most unfair to force them to go back on relief. They constitute a group which will have to be given special consideration. I should like to have answers from the -minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I shall be glad to answer, indeed. In the first place, this afternoon the hon. -member raised a point in connection with service rendered wholly in Canada. I would point out that in deciding when disability resulting from disease arose out of -or was directly connected with such military service, the commission takes into account any or all of the following factors:
Nature of service; the history of origin of the disease as revealed by the available evidence; the record of examination on- enlistment; the nature of the disease; the age of the individual; corroboration of statements.
Each case, in the final analysis, is considered on its merits, but recognition is given to the fact that conditions of service are more exacting than in civil life, and the individual is to a greater degree than in normal pursuits exposed to inclement weather, unusual mental and physical strain, and exposure to persons suffering from infectious diseases or carriers of infectious organisms. These are the considerations.
Is that under subsection 2 of section 11?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes.
Of course the act still remains the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes; but the administration- has been more or less altered along the lines I have indicated.

If the administration has been eased up, then surely the act should be eased up.
3072	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and Health

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I was just answering my hon. friend's question. That is the first answer, and it goes a long way to meet the objection raised.
Then, as to hospital allowances, I will deal with the type of cases as they normally occur on discharge from the forces:
(1)	If, in the opinion of medical officers of the Department of National Defence, he is, by reason of physical fitness, unlikely to be able to serve again, he is discharged.
From the army?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Yes. To continue:
(2)	If he requires treatment at that time, it is continued by the Department of Pensions and National Health. During such treatment he and his dependents receive exactly the same pay and allowances as paid during service except in the ease of officers holding the rank above that of sublieutenant (navy), lieutenant (military), or flying officer (air) who are paid at a rate not in excess of that applicable to a sublieutenant, lieutenant or flying officer.
In other words, their pay and allowances are cut down?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Yes; that is right. These allowances may be continued for a period of one year or for a period equal to the length of service, whichever is the less, provided always that treatment is required for that period. The allowances are payable not only while the man is in hospital but while on out-patient treatment or while convalescing and unable to work.
(3)	If further treatment is required and the disability is deemed by the pension commission to be pensionable, hospital allowances are thereafter paid at rates based on the 100 per cent pension rate for the rank held by the patient while in the forces, less $30 a month. That was established some years ago.
Suppose a disability is not pensionable; what happens at the end of the year?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I will come to that.
(4)	If at any time within a year following discharge from the forces, a man requires treatment for any condition whatsoever, other than a pensioned one-
That is during the year?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
-he may be given such treatment and, in addition, is paid allowances on behalf of him-

self and dependents equal to out-of-work benefits and training allowances payable under the reestablishment order.
In other words, he does not get his army pay?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

speechtext: In other words, he would get only $14.	*

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

speechtext:
Does the minister not think it would be a sounder and fairer practice to pay a man pay and allowances until he is discharged to civilian life? At a conference of the national council of veteran associations in Canada, held early last December in Toronto, which included representatives from the Sir Arthur Pearson Association of War Blinded, the Canadian Pensioners' Association, Canadian Corps Association and the Army and Navy Veterans in Canada, the following resolution dealing with treatment regulations was passed:
That in no case should the pay and allowance of a former member of the forces of this war in hospital be less than that of his rank during service for the whole of his period of initial and continuous treatment.
I suggest that that practice should have been carried out from the start instead of getting away to these different provisions and classifications.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
That was done for an obvious reason. The practice in the last war was entirely different. At that time we had a military hospitals commission and what my hon. friend now suggests should be done was done. A member of the forces undergoing treatment was on the strength of the defence forces, the militia forces or the armed forces until discharge. When the war was concluded we had many
problems to face. We found that in the interregnum certain abuses had occurred which, as my hon. friend will recall, resulted in the amendments of 1936. It was found that certain senior officers were receiving extravagant allowances. This fact came to the notice of the house and the amendments were passed with great acclaim in 1936.
I frankly confess that I see quite a lot of merit in the suggestion which my hon. friend has quoted as having been passed by this organization and which he supports himself. My reaction is that for a reasonable time after discharge until the soldier or the officer-
Prom the army or from the hospital?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I am thinking now of his return to civil life from the hospital. For a reasonable time he should be entitled to draw pay and allowances after military discharge while undergoing treatment and until he is reestablished. He should receive his pay as lieutenant, major or whatever rank he holds until we have effected complete establishment at home. But that practice should not be perpetuated once a man has been reestablished. I think we must then come back to a basis such as we have now.
.The pay and allowances in some cases would be less than a private would get in the army.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I do not think they are; they all come under the ceiling of lieutenant's pay. I frankly confess that there is a strong argument for the recommendation made by this organization. As a matter of fact we now have a committee in the department reviewing every single feature of treatment. This is under the chairmanship of Brigadier General Ross, with Doctor Bain, director of medical services, and Walter Woods, associate deputy minister. There are no finer three men in the whole service. This committee is giving careful consideration- to every possible phase of treatment and I will do my best to carry out whatever recommendations they may make as to any inequalities they may discover.

I should
like to say a few words about the section in the Pension Act which provides that a man's disability or deterioration in health must be attributable to service before he is entitled to a pension. I have a case in mind which I took up with the minister. He did make an educational grant to this particular fellow which has helped him out considerably, but
3074	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
he was refused a pension on the ground that his physical condition was not attributable to service.
When I was home this young fellow came to see me with his father and they outlined the whole case to me. It appears that when the boy joined up he referred to his disability which had occurred in early childhood. This was noted on his record, but that condition had not affected him for something like fifteen or sixteen years; to all appearances he had entirely outgrown it when he passed the medical board on joining the army. He was placed in category A-l, and when the attention of the medical authorities was drawn to the fact that he had suffered this disability in his early years they were particularly cautious. As I understand it, they reexamined him to see if he was really physically fit.
The doctors on the examining board have an opportunity to examine a man thoroughly before he joins the army. They have the advantage of the latest and best equipment. They are practical, experienced doctor's and they can make a thorough diagnosis. After this boy had joined up for active service and had passed A-l, he was turned out of the army physically unfit after a period of eight, ten or twelve months, I just forget the exact time. I believe that he was placed in category E, because in between that time he had been in the hospital for a long period.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
What is the nature of his disability?
Mr. JOHNSTON (Bow River); I am sorry I have not the file with me, but I know that in general the facts I am stating are correct. First of all, this boy wrote to me that he wanted a pension and the educational grant. I suggested that probably it would be better to get the educational grant first and later take up the question of a pension. I took up the question of an educational grant for him with the minister, through whose kindness we got that through, but there was quite a bit of red tape about it. The father sent me a letter expressing his appreciation and he asked me to convey his thanks to the minister, which I did, as the minister probably recalls. The point is that this boy when he tried to get a pension was refused on the ground that his condition was not attributable to. service, despite the fact that when he joined up he had a thorough medical examination and the medical diagnosis showed that he was A-l. I do not see what better authority we could have than the expert opinion of the doctors who examined him. The condition did not recur until after he joined the army, a matter of ten or twelve or thirteen years. I am not a medical doctor, but common 
sense tells one that the sickness which followed after he j oined up must have been entirely dhe to the conditions under which he was living, perhaps the strenuous training, while on active service. There is no doubt in my mind that it was his military service which caused his sickness, and it does not seem fair to me that the obligation of the government should be evaded in a case of that kind. Once the doctors pass a man as A-l, if anything happens to him afterwards it should be considered attributable to service and it should not debar him from receiving a pension. I think the minister would do well to reconsider that class of cases, which has been mentioned by others. It does seem to me to be most unfair.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Does my hon. friend remember whether it was a case of neurosis or a straight physical disability?
I should not like to say because I have not the file before me.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: My hon. friend, the member for Vancouver South, asked a question about the veterans' guard which I forgot to answer. I quite agree with the submission he made. These men are entitled to every consideration that we can give them. They are now getting close to sixty years and have served through two wars; some of them have undergone considerable hardship and they are certainly entitled to every consideration. We have a special subcommittee of the general committee on demobilization giving attention to their case. What will be worked out I cannot say. But we have not forgotten the suggestion which my hon. friend made when he was speaking this afternoon.
My other question was about changes in the Pension Act being made by order in council.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
We are doing what was done in the last great war to meet emergent conditions which arise from time to time. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre mentioned that it might endanger some of the benefits, but I can assure him that that will not be done. In the great war all this was done by order in conucil. It is most difficult to visualize the numerous changes that may have to take place in the pension system and in the war veterans' allowance before the war is over. The ideal way would be to pass a consolidated Pension Act and a consolidated War Veterans' Allowance Act, bringing all the amendments up to date and possibly incorporating others that have not yet received the

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
endorsation of this house. But orders in council are passed to meet emergent conditions. Otherwise we should have to amend the act three or four times a year.
These changes made by order in council affect the men of the last war, not of this war.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: My hon. friend is not opposed to them, I am sure.

No; but they should be put through in the form of amendments to the Pension Act; they have nothing to do with the men of this war.
Mr. MACKENZIE (Vancouver Centre); One of the first duties of parliament after hostilities cease will be to consolidate the Pension Act and various other pieces of soldier legislation, the Veterans' Allowance Act, the Veterans' Land Act and such others as will need consolidation.
I did not get an answer to my question with regard to disability incurred during service but not pensionable. What treatment can a man who is in that position get?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Under section 11 (3)?

No. A man incurs a disability during service, and it is held not pensionable because it did not arise directly out of his service. What treatment can that man get in hospital, and for how long, and what allowance can he get?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: After the first year of civil life he is entitled to treatment only if he is awarded a pension, unless he saw service in a theatre of actual war.
Otherwise he gets nothing?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is it.

As one listens to the minister one would imagine that all is well. Perhaps the cases that came to my attention are the unfortunate ones. I drew to the attention of the minister a particular case where a man was not being treated properly and the minister promptly rectified the trouble. It appears to me that these cases should not occur in the first place. I brought to the minister's attention recently the case of a sergeant who had enlisted for active service and after two years' service in Canada was injured in training. He took sick last September. That
was the first illness he had had. He was discharged in December. His sickness was diagnosed as diverticulitis. Since his discharge the man has had to go back to hospital, and the hospital authorities say that there is absolutely nothing they can do for him. All he has to do is to diet. He has to go home now and diet himself there. He has a wife and child whom he cannot support because of his disability. What I do not like about the case is this. When this man appeared in Saskatoon the members of the pension board informed him that he could receive no pension because he had not been overseas. It seems to me that the members of the board should be instructed to inform the men correctly as to what their position is, and that under certain conditions of service in Canada the man is pensionable.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Will my hon. friend send me the man's number?
His number is L.84656.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Was it a congenital condition?
Not to my knowledge.

The hon. member for Bow River made a remark which suggests a condition that I think should not exist. He said that through the kindness of the minister a man was able to get an educational grant. I have found on many occasions that if it had not been for the kindness of members of parliament on both sides of the house many men in the armed forces would not have been able to get their war veterans' allowance.	[DOT]
Why?

That is just it. Why? I know of many men who have written to myself or to other members about their cases. They could get no action upon them until some member of parliament intervened and took the case up for them. I want to say that the pension department has been extremely kind to me and has helped me out in all the cases I have brought to its attention. I am very much obliged, but I think the department should have some procedure whereby these men, when they need it, will get some action without the intervention of members of parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
I think the real explanation is that these cases come to the attention of hon. members, or possibly to my attention through the good will of hon. members, before they are ever referred to the pension board or other branches

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
of the government. The member of parliament is in the district; he knows the local conditions; he knows of cases of hardship; and I find frequently that when cases coming from hon. members of all parties are immediately referred to the departmental officials, sometimes, if not invariably, they have never come to the attention of the officials before.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Domiciliary care, sometimes called veterans' care.

In one case which came to my attention a veteran wanted to go there. He was receiving a war veterans' allowance at that time of, I think, $25, and they wanted to take the full $2s! He objected strongly, and he did not go, because he felt that he should have some money left over with which to buy little luxuries that he wanted, such as cigarettes or other extras.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: May I interrupt my hon. friend, just to be cooperative? Was that not a case of somebody drawing a pension? It was not a veterans' allowance, because he must have been a pensioner to qualify for domiciliary care.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

speechtext: That is quite a recent provision, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No; it is for comforts and clothing. It has been in effect for some time, I think.
In the case of all soldiers now on veterans' allowance, is it now raised right up to the peak automatically? It was not before.
1 think I made a statement in the house last year, when the increases were announced, that they would be automatic and would not require any intervention by the applicant.

Mention has been made of demobilization. Some months ago I heard the high commissioner for South Africa speak in Toronto. He said that no one in South Africa is demobilized until a job is secured for him. I thought that was an idea which Canada should adopt, because if we did, we would not have any unemployed men-or women-from the armed forces. That is a circumstance to take into consideration. The high commissioner also said that no wounded man is demobilized until a job is secured for him, and that casualties are centralized in camps at full pay. That is different from what it is here.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No. I believe our ideas, which have not yet been finalized, are moving along the same lines.
They will come to that?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
In that connection, may I place a short extract upon the record? It is proposed that the Department of Pensions and National Health should establish rehabilitation facilities at each demobilization centre, and that all personnel should be interviewed by competent interviewers as a primary screening, and thence referred to one or other of the following sections, which will be operated by trained counsellors of the department: (a) vocational training section; (b) interrupted education section; (c) information officer of the Veterans' Land Act administration; (d) civil service commission representative for persons interested in dominion government employment; (e) representative of the unemployment insurance commission, with regard to employment; (f) representatives of the pensions and treatment branches of the Department of Pensions and National Health; (g) special consultants in cases presenting problems which deviate from the normal; (h) special counsellor for female members of the forces, and (i) special counsellor for disabled men. For this purpose it is deemed essential

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
that personnel and educational officers in the three branches of the service, plus the necessary clerical staff to be drawn from the services, should be given preference in employment in the rehabilitation branch of the Department of Pensions and National Health and the administration of the Veterans' Land Act. It is considered that after primary screening and secondary consultation as has just been outlined, persons to be discharged will resolve themselves broadly into the following groups: (1) those who have a job to go to, or those who are engaged in a business or profession on their own account; (2) those who are accepted for vocational training under existing provisions; (3) those who are accepted for resumption of interrupted education at university level; (4) those who desire to be released with a view to returning to their own farms, and those who desire to make application for settlement on the land and are able to make provision for themselves until their eligibility is determined. It is thought that these four groups should be released as soon as arrangements can be made for the carrying on of the new business, training, or settlement on the land, or, if they are able to make provision for themselves pending the completion of such arrangements, it is thought that they might be discharged even earlier.
This leaves two major groups: those who are fully competent and skilled and require no training; and unskilled persons lacking the basic education to assimilate a training course. These latter groups should be referred to the employment office of the unemployment insurance commission, with a view to placement in employment.
It is a corollary of the programme which I have just described that those who are not immediately able to enter upon, for instance, vocational training, or for whom employment is not immediately available, should not be discharged from the forces until the arrangements contemplated for them have been completed.
The procedures that have been described 'will apply both to new recruits and personnel with short service in Canada, as well as to personnel returned from overseas.
The foregoing procedure covers those who can be absorbed by former employment, training, and farming, on their own resources.
With respect to those who cannot be so absorbed, it will be the responsibility of the government of the day, in cooperation with private industry through the facilities of the proposed department of reconstruction, to develop additional avenues of employment.
To the extent that such additional employment opportunity is not available, the device of retarded demobilization may be the necessary solution.
These are just some of the suggestions that have come before the committees who have been giving anxious thought and care to this problem.
The problem of demobilization really falls into three parts: First, the problem of repatriation, which is the task of the defence forces, that is getting the men home after hostilities are over. This may occupy a considerable time. Second, the problem of demobilization, which will be a joint problem between the defence services who are in charge of the men until they are handed over to the Department of Pensions and National Health for active rehabilitation in after life. Third, the problem of rehabilitation itself, which will be the primary concern of the Department of Veterans' Affairs.
Are these suggestions put forward as those which will be the, policy of the government, or are they suggestions?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: They are suggestions. They are not finalized yet, but these are suggestions made by certain committees which for the last year and a half have been giving very careful attention to this matter.

Further with regard to this talk which I heard from the High Commissioner of South Africa. He said that in South Africa, when a job was secured for a man or woman demobilized from the forces, he or she must be kept on the payroll for at least six months. That is a good suggestion, because there is the chance during the six months for that man to "find his feet". Over there they are using prisoners of war to prepare the farms which will be available under this land settlement act for soldiers.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Veterans Land Act.

Yes.
If the returned men went on some of the farms that I have seen, which are being taken over by the government for these men, they would find it very difficult for some time to make a living on them because in many cases the buildings need repairs, and there is a suggestion that if we had someone to put these farms into shape the soldier or airman or the man from the navy would have a better break. I do not know whether it was from the minister's department, but over the radio
3078	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
some months ago I heard the closing part of a speech with reference to amputation cases which struck me rather forcibly. The speech in question ended something like this: Ordinary people are looking for an extraordinary place in life, whereas the amputation cases are extraordinary people who are looking only for an ordinary place in life. I thought how true that was, because these fellows simply want to be reestablished.
What is being done with regard to the staff houses that are not being used any longer by Wartime Housing? Is the department going to take them over for hospitals? We have a wonderful institution of this kind in Peterborough and I should like to see it turned into a hospital.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: My recollection is that when some of these were being given up I got into touch with the officials of the department to make a survey of all the facilities in connection with staff houses and air training centres to see if they could be used for any of the essential purposes of the department, but I am sorry to say that the results were not very encouraging. The Department of Labour is making a survey of such places with a view to having them utilized for vocational training purposes when this scheme is going fully on the return of the men. How far we have gone with that survey I do not know, but as regards the medical treatment end of it the report was not very encouraging.
Would these places not be all right for convalescent cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Convalescent homes as such we have not under the department and have never had. The only feature of the work of the department by way of treatment that approaches convalescent homes is the domiciliary care which I mentioned; that is to say, the care of veterans. We have one in Toronto and one in Vancouver, and from 100 to 200 men are happy in their later years in these places. We may have to extend them, but we do not call them convalescent homes. The new policy of the department in connection with such conditions is rather to help and there are five centres under contemplation-possibly more. We are starting with one, and I hope that before the session is over all hon. members will take occasion to examine thoroughly the one at Rideau Centre in the vicinity of Ottawa. The idea is to foster the desire on the part of the men for work once again after their war experiences by which they have been shaken. In addition to that, there will be definite

need of a psychiatric centre and the extension of small convalescent homes, though I do not like that name; I prefer to call them veterans' care homes. We are now in touch with those who have been doing excellent work for the air force and the army. They have convalescent homes throughout the country, raised by private subscription through the good will of public-spirited citizens, and we may be able to obtain some of these later on.
Mr. FRASER (Peterborough West); Is the one in Ottawa now under construction?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: It is known as Rideau Centre.

Is the guild of all arts in Toronto under the minister's direction?
Mr. MACKENZIE (Vancouver Centre); Yes; that is a special psychiatric centre after the pattern of Mill Hill in England, which has had a tremendous success.
It is under the minister's department?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Yes.
We are trying to stick as close as possible to the estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I am afraid not.

Well, the members of this group are. We are trying to deal with principles rather than details. The minister will remember that a year ago when he last had his estimates before the committee I suggested to him that, because of the nature of the war, we would require a considerable expansion in our neurological hospitals across the country. The minister agreed at that time and intimated that they had this in mind. Now, a year later, he says that the establishing of psychiatric centres throughout Canada is still a matter of consideration, with a start being made, I understand, in one or two places.
I wish to direct to his attention a matter we discussed last year, and to demonstrate the necessity of the principle I will state a case for him. It is a case I discussed last year in the house. A boy received a fractured skull while thrown from a jeep. For the past year he has been going through the process of proving his claim and he did succeed in entering Camp Hill hospital. He had had a partial stroke. The decision at the hospital was that he was suffering from psychosis, and because of the fact that he had not been examined by a pensions medical examiner and

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
assessed for pension he was shifted to an insane asylum. That man, in my opinion, and I believe in any one else's opinion, is in no condition to be placed, and should not under any circumstances be placed, in a regular insane asylum for treatment. To the best of my knowledge, there are in that institution no facilities and perhaps not the skilled personnel necessary to treat a case of that kind. I suggest that he should have been removed to Montreal to one of the neurological hospitals there.
I bring this to the minister's attention because it definitely proves that in most sections of Canada there is not the kind of institutional care necessary for such cases. The letter I have received in connection with this case is dated May 16. It comes from the pensions medical examiner in Camp Hill hospital. He states that this man is suffering from psychosis, having been admitted on April 25, 1944, and transferred to the Nova Scotia Mental hospital at Dartmouth on April 27, 1944, and at the present time he is undergoing treatment there under the new clause 2, which is the old clause 20. I believe that disability is admitted as attributable to service. While in the institution he gets pay but he is not assessed for pension. My objection is to placing a boy with that sort of disability in such an institution.
There is another matter I wish to discuss and I shall be brief. In the matter of pensions for women serving in the auxiliary services, I suggest that they should be treated exactly as the service personnel in the men's section of the services. The same rates should apply. In the present regulation the differential that exists in the schedules or wage rates or whatever you want to call them has been carried forward into the pension schedules. Many of these girls are overseas and many of them are likely to suffer the same disabilities as the men. If on returning from overseas they have disabilities of ten per cent, fifteen per cent or twenty-five per cent, the rates which apply in the case of regular service personnel should certainly apply to them also. I think everyone in the house has admitted that in connection with the wage schedules generally there are good arguments why the women should be treated the same as the men. I merely leave that thought with the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: We did raise them quite recently from two-thirds to four-fifths.
Yes; but I think they should receive 100 per cent, at least in this matter of pensions.

We have made provision for the rehabilitation of certain groups coming back from overseas, but I have in mind one group in particular for whom no provision is made; I refer to business and professional men whose careers have been interrupted by the war. Has any consideration been given to granting capital loans in such cases? Take, for instance, a young lawyer who worked hard to get through college and who was in practice for perhaps only a year or two before entering the service. When he comes back he will have a very hard time to get going unless some provision is made for his rehabilitation. The same is true with respect to men in other lines of business, and I wondered if any consideration has been given along the line I have suggested.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Is my hon. friend referring to capital loans for the purpose of establishing such men in business?
Yes. I mention it because certain capital loans and grants are being made to men settling under the veterans' land act, and I wondered if something similar was being considered for men in business.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: That is also receiving consideration by a special committee of the demobilization committee.

Is a soldier granted a pension according to the application or presentation submitted by him, or is the pension decided on the evidence available in the case? Does it make any difference how the application is presented by the applicant; will the decision be the same in any event? I ask this question because there is a great difference in the ability of men to present a case, and I do not consider that a fair way of arriving at a decision. I believe that a case should be decided on its merits rather than on the ability of the applicant to present it. I have in mind the case of a man in my riding who served all through the last war. When the present war broke out he enlisted again and served for three years in England. He was knocked down by a motorcycle in a blackout one night, and injured to the extent that it was necessary to discharge him. If his pension is decided on his ability to present his case, I do not think he would get along very well.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Perhaps I should outline the procedure that is adopted. It is as follows:
(1)	When an application is first made for pension the commission reviews all relevant records including such documentary evidence as
3080	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
may be submitted and makes such inquiry through its medical and other officers as appears advisable into -the facts upon which the application is based, and if satisfied that the applicant is entitled to pension it makes such award and takes the necessary steps to cause the payment of pension to be made.
(2)	When the application is not granted the applicant is notified in writing of the decision with the grounds therefor, and advised that unless he makes an application for second hearing within ninety days the case will be closed.
(3)	If a second hearing is requested, the commission informs the applicant in writing:
(a) That if he so desires 'he may have the assistance of the veterans' bureau free of charge, or a service bureau of a veterans' organization, or -by some other person at his own expense in the preparation and presentation of his application;
(-b) That a summary of all available evidence will foe mailed to him -by the veterans' bureau; and
(c) That his complete claim must be submitted within a period of six months of the date of mailing of the summary of evidence.
(4)	The commission also notifies -the veterans' *bureau that an application -for second hearing has been accepted, and the veterans' bureau thereupon prepares a summary of all available evidence and mails a copy to the applicant.
(5)	When the applicant notifies -the commission within a period of six months that he is satisfied to submit his claim, the commission makes its ruling on second hearing.
(G) If the ruling on second hearing is not favourable to the applicant the commission notifies the applicant accordingly in writing, stating the grounds therefor, and informs him that if he so desires he may appear before an appeal board of the commission, provided that he so requests within ninety days.
(7)	For the purpose of hearing applications an appeal board of the commission consists of three members and holds sittings periodically throughout places in Canada. The members of such appeal boards are designated by the chairman of the commission, -but shall not include any member of the commission who has previously ruled on first or second hearing of the application. At such hearings appeal 'board representations may be made in person and sworn verbal evidence adduced.
(8)	The decision of such appeal board shall be final except that an application may be made -to a special appeal board of the commission on the grounds of error, or by reason of evidence not having been produced to the commission for leave to reopen the application.
This is the result of many years of discussion by veterans' organizations, and I think it is a fairly successful procedure.
Is there any hospital for exservice men between Vancouver and Calgary?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Not definitely, as such, except the contract hospitals with which we have made arrangements for their care.

Last session I endeavoured to impress upon the minister the dire need of some accommodation, either by way of a

hospital or convalescent homes, in the interior, for the reason that the distance between Vancouver and Calgary is just one thousand miles, which is a long stretch for invalids to travel. From the interior we have sent overseas fully five thousand men, more than tw-o thousand coming from the staff of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting company alone. No more beautiful location for a veterans' home or hospital could be found than on the shores of Lake Kootenay, where there is an- ideal climate and every conceivable recreation. It would seem only reasonable for the minister's advisers to give some consideration to hospital accommodation in the interior. Just to illustrate my point, in the latter part of 1939 we had a member of the 111th battery discharged from hospital in Edmonton. He came to Nelson, where he had enlisted, went into hospital for a month, and then was taken to his home some thirty miles distant. Then it became necessary for him to receive immediate hospital care, and they had to send- back to Nelson- for an ambulance. It cost the parents of that boy some 845 to have him taken to the nearest hospital, which would be in Denver, about thirty miles away. When he sought to recover the cost of the ambulance he was told that he should have gone to the Shaughnessy hospital in Vancouver. The minister will realize the impossibility of moving a boy in a critical condition a distance of five hundred miles, where there is hospital accommodation available within thirty miles. Does the minister countenance this sort of thing? Is it not possible to care for returned men- in local hospitals when they require hospitalization?

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health

I should like to support and endorse with all my heart what the hon. member who has just taken his seat has said. After all, we do represent the beauty spots of Canada. Healthy, well people travel thousands of miles to enjoy the invigorating air and the beauty of the scenery which alone is to be found in the valleys of the Rockies. It would seem almost trite to say that if the surrounding scenery and invigorating air contribute to the well-being, spiritual as well as physical, of the normal healthy man, it would have an even greater and more beneficial effect upon one who has sweated, toiled and laboured in the defence of us who are more fortunate and remain here at home.
I have often wondered why there are no rest homes anywhere between Calgary and Harrison Hot Springs in the Rocky mountains. And yet there are objections which I can well see might be advanced. I do know-and I shall make further reference to it on another occasion-that when veterans come home they do not want to be isolated, or placed awTay from their fellowmen. However, there are centres in the mountains, places such as Banff. Lake Louise and Nelson, all charming and delightful spots in themselves, and inhabited by people generous to a degree, from whom the sick or the convalescent soldier would receive that care and friendship which contribute so much to speedy recovery.
Without casting any reflection upon anyone who may be so unfortunate as to have to live in one of our metropolitan centres, I venture to say that the convalescent soldier, the sick man, will find more of the warmth of human sympathy and kindness in those smaller towns and cities, yea, in the villages, if you will, or in the wide open spaces of the prairies or the foothills or the mountain valleys, than he will find anywhere else in Canada. At Nelson, at Banff or at Lake Louise, where our transportation companies have invested millions for the well-being of people who will visit there, we as a nation might very well spend some money in building rest homes and hospitals for those who have given the best years of their lives for us.
In that connection I would refer to another matter connected with pensions and national health. May I say how much the people of Calgary appreciate the good judgment and discernment of the department in locating at Calgary what I have every reason to believe is probably the finest military hospital of its kind to be found anywhere on this continent, or probably in the world. It is a credit to Canada and to the department. In that hospital is to be found every modern convenience known to medicine and surgery for the care
and treatment of our returned soldiers. It stands in striking contrast to the miserable accommodation provided for the heroes of the last war. I congratulate the minister and the department upon their sparing no pains, money or scientific knowledge in the lay-out of that hospital, and I commend them, too, for the care and attention our returned soldiers are now receiving at the hands of the department.
I have only one other suggestion to make, and it has to do with the problem of rehabilitation and the integration into civilian life of our returned men. For the last four years- and it may extend to five years-our men overseas have been trained in the arts of war and the habits of military life. To whom do they look, and to whom have they looked for the last four years for counsel and advice in regard to their physical, social, domestic and military problems? I believe it is correct to say that in ninety per cent of cases they look to their officers. They look to the officers who command them, the officers to whose commands they respond. When the war is over, the control of those officers will be gone. No longer will the men have any right to look to them; no longer will the officer have any right to command. I wonder if we are not missing something in our plans and our programmes if we do not give consideration to the retention of the services of that officer, who has been the leader of those men and that he should be the last man discharged from the armed forces. Should we not retain the services of those officers in order that they may minister to, counsel and advise the soldiers and the noncommissioned officers who have served under them? Is there not some way whereby we can retain the services of the officer for his men?
I appreciate, as I am sure most hon. members do, that seventy-five per cent, or perhaps even a higher percentage of the men who will be rehabilitated into civilian life will have little difficulty. But there will be a remaining fifteen to twenty-five per cent who in normal, ordinary peace-times were, and will continue to be, if you will, problem cases. They had difficulties. They were not able to fend for themselves; they had difficulty in finding their niche. They were the men who relied upon their more -experienced fellow citizens to counsel and advise them. They are people who were in the habit of having to be told what to do. Can we not by some means retain the services of the officers in our armed forces for the benefit of those men, so that they may counsel and advise?
My next thought is connected with public health. We have heard considerable discussion respecting a serious problem, particularly in the rural areas of Canada, more particularly

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
those of western Canada. During the Easter recess I attended a meeting at which two doctors were present. One of them to come to this meeting-and, frankly, it was a political meeting-had driven 125 miles. The other one had driven approximately sixty miles and thought nothing of it. This one doctor serves a territory with a radius of approximately 125 miles centering on his home, and yet he has to supplement his income from his professional services by engaging in the raising of stock such as cattle and hogs, and the growing of grain. I commended his enterprise. He is a man beloved and highly regarded in his community, but what is the answer to this problem? He is staying there from a sense of duty and obligation to these people.
It seems to me that we ought to help people to get medical services. In this day and age we should not insist upon a doctor living in a rural community where he cannot make a comfortable or decent living, where he cannot take advantage of modem hospitals and equipment. Why cannot we take the doctor to the people who require his services, or bring those people to the doctor by modern methods and means? At one time, between Calgary and Banff, a distance of eighty-five miles, there were four doctors. One was located at Cochrane, one at Exshaw, another at Canmore and another at Banff. What happened? The doctor at Cochrane has ceased to practice. Why? With the advent of the automobile people who were critically ill would drive past his door to go to Calgary where they could get better hospitalization and, as they thought, more skilled attention. The same thing happened at Exshaw, and now there is no doctor at either place. The result is that Calgary is serving an area seventy-five miles to the west. Toward the northwest many people live from 125 to 200 miles from a doctor.
I suggest that there should be attached to each medical centre a modern aeroplane with a competent pilot to serve an area with a radius of at least 200 miles. The aeroplane could take the doctor to patients needing his services or, if it were urgent, bring the patient to the medical centre. From time to time we hear and read of "mercy flights" in western Canada, but we should not regard them as exceptional any longer. Why not answer the call of modern times and use some of our aircraft for this purpose? I think it is a deplorable situation that professional brains and ability should have to spend time driving across our prairies in a Ford or Chevrolet automobile when the same distance could be covered by an aeroplane in ten or fifteen minutes.

If the minister has not already given consideration to this matter I suggest that he should consider giving financial aid if necessary to the provinces in order that they may modernize and stream-line their medical services. The armed services in Italy and the air force on our sea coasts, as well as the navy, are doing this sort of thing to-day. We have an abundant supply of modem aircraft which could be adapted to that purpose and used to take the doctor to his patient or bring the patient to the doctor, and thereby save time and suffering and conserve and distribute medical skill and hospital facilities.
